speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a number of citizens in the National Capital Region have united to ask that all levels of government in the area proclaim this Public Servants' Day. On behalf of the federal Government I would like to salute the contribution which public servants make to the quality of life in the National Capital Region.

The federal Government is the region's biggest employer, employing over 74,000 public servants in many different fields. I am thinking, for instance, of scientists, clerks, meat inspectors, museum curators, architects, marine biologists, veterinarians and word processor operators, to name only a few. They all contribute to the quality of life in the National Capital.
In addition, another 40,000 residents in the region are employed by provincial or municipal governments. The general public does not generally make subtle distinctions between these various levels of government, and that is why, today, I think it is appropriate to take this opportunity and join provincial and municipal governments serving this region in paying tribute to our public servants.

A word of thanks is due to the organizers of this event. With volunteer help they have promoted this day throughout the region so that public servants at all levels of government might be the recipients of a well-deserved tribute. I would also like to extend my thanks and the thanks of the Government, not only to the public servants here in the National Capital Region but to all of those equally deserving Canadian public servants who are working all across Canada and abroad.
Seldom do we have the opportunity or the occasion, as a major employer, to thank our staff. I would like to take this opportunity to do just that. Thank you, ladies and gentlemen,
for the quiet dedication and professionalism you have shown in serving the Canadian public.

Dare say that I wonder about the spirit of Meech Lake when I see this kind of cavalier treatment meted out to those who must implement the policy of getting to our two major language groups service from the federal Government.
Finally, I also believe that any government that has the true interests of its employees at heart would have long ago realized that the pension de-indexation in Bill C-33 is completely out of step with developments in pensions policy in the private sector and should be dropped.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the New Democratic Party, I led off this debate, but because of the Royal Assent to certain Bills I did not complete my remarks and I still have left a few minutes of the time allotted to me for my speech.
I want to deal with one more aspect of this proposal which I consider important, that is the downside of this proposal to privatize Eldorado and the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation. We heard of the supposedly good reasons from the Minister. However, what the Minister did not tell us is that in order for this privatization to go forward, in order for this stock flotation deal to succeed-and that is all it really is-the public sector will underwrite the risks inherent in this deal by assuming the debt of Eldorado Nuclear Limited and the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation.
The federal Government will also assume the further liability of Eldorado's nuclear waste problems at Port Hope at a cost of perhaps S75 million.
This take-back of debt has been described by the financial advisers to the Government as necessary for the success of the flotation. Eldorado's debts are substantial. We have calculated them in the range of $550 million. The federal Government will receive from the newly merged company approximately $250 million, leaving $300 million of debt which must be made up in the sale of shares in the new company before the Government breaks even on its debt obligation alone. This has nothing to do with the accumulative investment in Eldorado in the form of government equity. Therefore, the Government needs a high share price or it will wind up with a brick in its hands, something like the British Columbia resources privatization put through by the Bennett Government which issued shares at $5 and which now trade for about 90 cents. There is no evidence that this privatization deal will be any more successful.
We have to ask ourselves if there is any certainty of a high share price. Uranium markets are currently in chronic oversupply and prices are depressed. If the United States were once more to close its market to foreign producers in response to the distress of its domestic suppliers, conditions would be chaotic and, of course, the trade deal would do nothing for Canadian producers caught in this bind.
We know that uranium producers in the United States, like our friends in the Canadian Government and Canadian business, are gung-ho to see the free trade deal go through, but the reality is that if their interests are pinched, the uranium producers in the United States will become just like any other private corporation. One cannot blame them, when they see the competition they are getting and will get from Canada, for screaming that Canadian producers are being subsidized by the Government and there ought to be limits put on the sale of uranium to the United States. There are no guarantees that
the federal Government will get its investment in Eldorado back, let alone cover the debts of Eldorado.
What are the other advantages or disadvantages of this deal? 1 talked about this in the earlier part of my speech. There are really no job guarantees. In fact, rather the opposite.
The Minister spoke of the rationalization of the two companies. Most companies know what rationalization means. "Rationalization" means being more efficient, and being more efficient means fewer workers, and fewer workers means layoffs. If the Government does not realize this, the unions certainly do. They have a desire to protect the workers in this industry. They are, to say the least, very doubtful about this whole proposal.
I want to deal with one other issue. The claim has been made so often with respect to the uranium industry that somehow Governments which operate companies as public corporations cannot be efficient and cannot look after the interests of their shareholders, in this case, the people of Canada, and that somehow privatization will be much more efficient and so on. Nothing could be further from the truth, as a matter of principle, and particularly when it comes to the uranium industry.
One does not have to be a wild-eyed socialist who believes in public ownership of everything to say that the uranium industry is a perfect example of how private industry is not efficient,and how private industry could only have existed by massive subsidies from the people and Governments of Canada.
Anyone who doubts that claim need only look at an article which appeared in Canada's national newspaper, The Globe and Mail, a few days ago on April 9. The article was entitled, "The less-than-holy Roman empire", written by Paul McKay. Mr. McKay has done a much better job than I could hope to do. I wish to put on the record some of the points made by Mr. McKay. It is as devastating a critique of a privately owned corporation as I have ever seen; its lack of concern for the welfare of its workers, its insistence on being guaranteed that in no way would that company lose money, its insistence on the part of its president, that great exponent of the free enterprise system, Stephen Roman, that he could only continue by the most massive continued and constant major subsidies by the public, by the Government of Canada, and by the Government of Ontario through Ontario Hydro.
Let me put on the record some of the points made by Paul McKay in his article:
Medical records and royal commissions have shown that a pathetic army of the miners Mr. Roman employed at his uranium mines in Elliot Lake, Ontario, have gone to their own early graves because their lungs were needlessly poisoned with radioactivity and mine dusts-a company that refused to spend more than a pittance on mine safety equipment and a wilful ignorance of study after study proving uranium miners were being ravaged by cancer and lung disease.



April 11, 1988

Let me ask a question. What assurances can we receive from the government that when we get rid of Eldorado Mining as a Crown corporation, where hopefully there was some consideration for the workers who worked for that company, the type of attitude and approach followed by Mr. Roman in Denison Mines will not be the policy of a new privately owned company, with the same complete disregard for the welfare of the workers shown by Mr. Roman?
Let me further quote from the article:
The truth is that Mr. Roman's uranium empire was founded on no-risk, guaranteed, cost-plus government weapons contracts, that his empire would not have survived its first 20 years without more than $1 billion in government subsidies, sweetheart contracts and special bail-outs, and that his company was pulled out of its last major tailspin with the help of a secret international uranium cartel.
This from a company whose president never got tired of preaching the benefits of the free enterprise system and condemning government intervention in the affairs of privately owned companies.
Let me further quote from the article:
.. . what the federal government, through Crown-controlled Eldorado Nuclear Ltd., was willing to sink into uranium properties. The package of subsidies included up-front development money, guaranteed sales at guaranteed prices, tax holidays, extravagant depletion allowances, millions of dollars' worth of free research and development work, and no capital gains tax if the property was sold within five years.
In short, Eldorado was promising a no-risk, no-tax, cost-plus contract if Mr. Roman could get his mine into production by 1957.
It is lucky for the Government, the Liberal Party, and for those believers in the free enterprise system that the type of facts which we know about this situation are not known by most ordinary Canadians. If they did know those facts, we would have a revolution about the type of unfair tax system which we have in this country.
One Member of Parliament called the deal to which I referred "the biggest piece of pie ever handed to private industry in the mining industry in Canada". Every ounce of the uranium produced by Denison Mines went into United States nuclear bombs; the amounts and prices were guaranteed.
The Government of France wanted to make a deal with Mr. Roman. It wanted to buy 50,000 tons of uranium over the next 25 years at a price in the $700 million range. Mr. Roman had a lot of trouble with that because the Government of France did not want to give the assurances which the then Canadian Government insisted upon, that the uranium would not be used for military purposes. The then Government of Canada said to Mr. Roman that it would not permit that deal, but that it would arrange it so that Ottawa, the Government of Canada, would buy lots of uranium, stockpile it, and hope for sunnier days. The biggest beneficiary of the two Government's stockpile programs in the 1960s, which were worth a total of $100 million, was Denison Mines owned by that great exponent of the free enterprise system, Mr. Roman.
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
In late 1970, a third stockpiling program worth $39 million was announced. A new Crown corporation, Uranium Canada, would be created to run it. In early 1972 there was a situation, because of the falling price of uranium, where the Government officials set in motion the notorious uranium cartel which, through a system of phoney price bids and market quotas, triggered a 700 per cent increase in the world price of uranium in less than four years.
Who was the major beneficiary? Mr. Roman. It was the biggest sweetheart deal of them all. A 30 year cost-plus multibillion dollar contract was arranged to supply uranium to Ontario Hydro, not at the price it should have been if the free enterprise system was working and where because there was a surplus of uranium the price should have come down; oh, no. Mr. Roman was very happy to participate in the government cartel which gave him a guaranteed price far higher than the price should have been.

subtopic: ELDORADO NUCLEAR LIMITED REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Bill before us respecting the proposed Eldorado Nuclear Limited reorganization and divestiture Act was introduced in the House by the then Minister of State for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs on March 29, an agreement having been reached between the Government of Canada and the Government of Saskatchewan in February to merge and privatize the assets of Eldorado Nuclear and the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation.
In outlining the reasons for the merger the Minister stated three criteria which she had in mind; first, that the Crown corporation was no longer serving a public interest or public policy function which needed to be carried out by government. Second, she stated the view that privatized corporations should be given what they need to be viable after privatization. I will return to this point, because it seems as though rather a lot is being given to the Government of Saskatchewan in this deal and one must question whether it is in the best interests of Canadians. Third, the Minister said that in arriving at the decision the interests of the employee and of public safety and the rights of Canadian taxpayers to have their financial interests protected were all considered. These are good principles, but we will want to ensure at committee that the rhetoric is in fact matched by actions on the part of the Government.
In 1983 the Liberal Government of the day transferred the shares of Eldorado Nuclear to the Canada Development Investment Corporation, and was also considering privatization. I myself consider that if the private sector can do well and responsibly anything that government is now doing, there is certainly a strong argument to transfer that function to the private sector.
However, with this Government, which on a number of occasions seems to be operating on the basis of ideology- rushing to privatization without careful examination of the economic costs, without careful consideration of environmental and other public policy goods-we will want to examine this transfer very carefully, indeed.
Eldorado Nuclear has been in existence for 61 years. It is the oldest uranium producer in the world. It is also the only integrated producer in Canada, which means that it can process ore to create uranium products for use in Canadian reactors to serve Canadian energy needs, as well as for export. It has new, modern, and efficient plants and owns and has interests in uranium mines.
The other partner, the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation, is also a large supplier of uranium, producing 7 per cent of the western world's capacity in 1986. It has sales contracts which extend well into the next decade. It has emphasized exploration and has some of the world's largest commercial reserves.
In her speech on March 29 the Minister said that a merger between the two would produce a company which would be not only viable but would also have the potential to grow and develop because of the amalgamation of assets including reserves, production facilities, and research.
We will have questions about this, to which I will come in a few minutes, because the deal, on the face of it and on the Minister's own information, will cost Canadian taxpayers a fair amount. That is not quite consistent with the very rosy picture being given of the benefits.
The Minister says that she wants control of this new company to remain in Canadian hands, and Article V of the Bill imposes constraints on the issue, transfer, and ownership of voting securities in the new company. We will want to examine these points very carefully to ensure that in fact Canadian ownership of this important resource is protected.
The Minister also pointed out quite correctly that the rules concerning waste disposal and the rules arising out of Canada's adherence to the non-proliferation treaty, the international treaty concerning control of nuclear energy products, apply equally to the private sector and to the public sector. However, the fact that the rules are in existence and the way they are applied are two different things, and we will have further questions about it.
The intention in the Bill is to set up a task force which will order the transition as we face the amalgamation of a Crown corporation of Canada and a Crown corporation of Saskatchewan.
In her speech introducing the Bill the Minister said that she was very proud of the two-stage merger and privatization process which she was proposing for Eldorado Nuclear. It will be important to see whether that pride is in fact justified or whether this will be another case of misplaced enthusiasm for privatization without the adequate mechanisms in force to ensure that it really is a benefit to Canadians.
On the face of it, as our energy critic, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan) pointed out, it is not strictly a business proposition. The deal would appear to be loaded in favour of the Province of Saskatchewan which is receiving a multimillion dollar package, courtesy of the federal Government. I have no objection to the Government deciding as part of a program for regional development to make a grant to the Government of Saskatchewan, but it should be clearly identified as such. It should not be disguised as a commercial transaction which is of equal value to all taxpayers in Canada.
Furthermore, when we look at the prices we find that Eldorado Nuclear has been undervalued and by an interesting process. For the purpose of this transaction, the assets of Eldorado Nuclear are placed at $915.9 million, while the assets of the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation are valued at $973.2 million. The Government of Canada will
April 11, 1988

have a 39.5 per cent share of the new company while Saskatchewan will have a 61.5 per cent interest. The new company will issue promissory notes valued at 40 per cent of the fixed assets to cover all of the debt owed to the Saskatchewan Government and only $230 million of the $570 million owed to the Government of Canada, so the promissory notes cover all of the debt of the Province of Saskatchewan but only about half of the debt of the Government of Canada. It seems that after this company is rolled over into one corporation and eventually sold to the private sector, the Province of Saskatchewan will have recovered all of its debt and losses while the Government of Canada will still be out $100 million.
It appears that in arriving at a value the two companies were evaluated from a discounted cash flow basis rather than from an asset basis. The Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation had a lower operating cost, primarily as a result of lower royalties but, interestingly, Eldorado was determined to be lower in value as a result of its less profitable refinery business. The refinery business was regarded as a detriment to the value of Eldorado Nuclear.
In the publicity surrounding this merger the two governments of Canada and Saskatchewan have said that one of the advantages of the merger is the capacity to process uranium in house. Let me quote directly from the joint press release:
A merger-will result in a company with an improved balance between its
mining and refining capacities.
This is very puzzling, Madam Speaker. On the one hand the value of Eldorado was downgraded in this transaction because the refinery was not profitable. On the other hand we are told that one of the great advantages, one of the great potentials for future profits of the merged company is the fact that the refinery exists. Which way is it? Is the refinery an advantage or not?
There are a number of other questions of this kind. There are clauses which seem, worrisomely, open ended about what the Government of Canada will put into this transaction. The Bill also leaves the Government of Canada liable for any debt or liability of Eldorado. There is no indication that there is legislation in Saskatchewan which leaves the Saskatchewan Government liable for any debts or obligations of the Saskatchewan partner.
We are left with many questions. What will be the actual cost to the taxpayers of Canada? What is the Government's position on disposal of low level waste? What is the commitment of the Government to ensure safety of handling of these materials at every point?
This merger will create the world's largest uranium producer with assets of $1.9 billion, but that market value is probably greater than Canadian investors can absorb. While the Minister has talked about the possibilities for Canadians to invest in this corporation, it is all very vague. At first blush we are left to wonder if there is any economic value whatever in this merger to the taxpayers of Canada, whether the merger
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
achieves anything except greater concentration in an industry which already has high concentration.
The new corporation will be responsible for disposing of low level radioactive wastes left by its predecessors up to a cost of $25 million and it is not clear who bears these costs. It is not clear that the question of safety has been addressed or will be addressed.
The Minister reported that the sale of shares would cover all of the debt owed to the federal and provincial Governments, but this is not clearly required in the legislation. Complete divestiture by the two governments is expected to be complete by 1995. I would stress that I am not against privatization in the uranium industry particularly. It is a cyclical and vulnerable industry and it seems reasonable that risks should be borne by private investors and not taxpayers, to a large extent. But this Bill before us is not achieving that end. It leaves the taxpayer holding a big burden while removing some of the controls of Government.
The whole question of the use and management of uranium and the disposal of waste products is probably one of the most important and serious environmental issues facing this country and it gets little or no attention in this Bill. By 1995, when it is expected that the whole matter will be in the private sector, we are asked to take it for granted that the private sector will have adequate standards to protect the life, health and safety of Canadians. There is no indication in this legislation that the Government will deal with that problem effectively.
While we will not oppose the principle of the Bill at second reading, that is, the privatization, we will certainly want very considerable amendments, standards and safety requirements built into it at committee stage, not only to protect the Canadian taxpayers' pockets but also to protect issues of safety and environmental control.

Madam Speaker, I thought that someone from the government side might want to rise to defend what they are doing, but I suppose I can understand that they might not want to do that.
I begin by acknowledging a certain ambiguity that I have experienced in this debate. We have here a classic example of what is wrong with privatization and particularly what is wrong with privatization as it has been implemented by this Government.
This is a classic case. The people of Canada and the people of Saskatchewan, through the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation, invested many, many millions of dollars over the years in these two corporations. As a result of the ideological commitment of this Government to privatization and the ideological commitment of the Saskatchewan Government to privatization, these two Crown corporations are to be merged and then privatized through the sale of shares in a way that involves the Canadian people and the Saskatchewan people, the Saskatchewan people being in double jeopardy because they have contributed to both corporations. These people are now picking up most of the risk because all the debts and liabilities are being picked up by the Government in order to make this particular privatization possible.
We see that this is not a case of the Canadian taxpayers benefiting from privatization. It is a case of whoever comes to be the shareholders and particularly the majority shareholders in this new company benefiting form the investment that has been made over the years by the Canadian people and the Saskatchewan people in these two corporations.
Having said that, I want to make it clear that it is not appropriate to be against privatization in every and all cases. I recall that not so long ago, in my own riding, a decision was made by the Manitoba Government to privatize Flyer Industries. In my judgment, at the time that decision was made, that was the thing to do. It was regrettable that the corporation faced the difficulties it did as a publicly-owned corporation, and some of the difficulties it faced were as a result of the fact that it was a publicly-owned corporation. These difficulties existed not through public ownership in and
April 11, 1988

of itself but because, as a result of it being a publicly-owned corporation, other and more powerful private companies in the bus market-place made life very difficult for that publicly-owned corporation.
One recalls that at one point in the 1970s the Ontario Conservative Government made it clear to municipalities, which were looking for transportation grants, that if they wanted grants for the purchase of buses they had better buy their buses from General Motors rather than from Flyer Industries in Manitoba, which was publicly owned. The last thing that the Conservatives wanted to see succeed was a publicly-owned bus company.
However, I stray from the point. We are talking about the privatization of Eldorado and the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation. I could not resist getting in that point about Flyer and the way in which the bias against public ownership on the part of the Conservative Party has, from time to time, led various federal and provincial Governments of their ilk not to let the market-place work, and publicly-owned companies to compete freely, but to try to skew the marketplace in such a way as to guarantee that these corporations would not succeed as well as they might in order that they could then point, with all due sanctimoniousness, to the fact that these corporations had not done as well as some had hoped. They then blamed it on public ownership instead of on their own intervention in the very market-place they say ought not to be intervened in.
On the question of privatization, I had the privilege of being in the British House of Lords one afternoon when the Earl of Stockton, the former Conservative Prime Minister of Great Britain, Harold MacMillan, now deceased, was giving a speech. He was speaking about the privatization program of Margaret Thatcher. I was very impressed with the ability of the former Prime Minister at the age of 92 to deliver a 20-minute speech without notes of any kind.
In his very articulate comments on the Government's privatization programs, he referred to the privatization of British Crown corporations being comparable to selling off a family's silver for short-term fiscal goals, creating a longer term situation of poorness in terms of assets and one's ability to determine one's own economic destiny, et cetera.
It was a very good speech and a good analogy of what this Government has been tempted to do. In many respects it has been selling off the family silver. Some of the privatizations with which the Government has gone ahead have been particularly ill-advised and have certainly fallen into the category of selling off the family silver. However, I am not absolutely sure about this one. This privatization shows what is wrong with privatization in the way in which the public picks up the risk and the private shareholders get the benefit.
Anyone who has been in this House for any time knows that I am not a great fan of the nuclear industry, uranium mining,
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
or nuclear power, all of the things involved in the economy with which these two corporations are tied. I would be less than frank if I did not say that I would just as soon that many of the things in which these corporation are involved were not happening, whether privately or publicly-owned.
One of the problems with the nuclear industry in this country has been that it has been so wrapped up in the public sector and the Government. Indeed, it was so close to both the Liberal bureaucracy and the Liberal Governments of the day that it is still impossible for Liberals in this House to say anything critical about the nuclear industry. That is their baby.
We had hoped that the Conservatives might have been more critical. They made a number of promises back in 1979, that they would have a full-scale inquiry into the nuclear industry in Canada. They made the same promise again in 1984. We pressed them on that in 1985 and 1986 and all we could get from the then Minister of Energy, who has since then been through several portfolios until she finally landed up in the Treasury Board, was that she would ask AECL whether it thought an inquiry was a good idea.
I think one must see the irony in a cabinet Minister of a Party which once promised an inquiry into this very Crown corporation and many of its activities rising in the House to say that she was thinking about an inquiry but was going to check with the Crown corporation to see whether or not it thought it was necessary. The Hon. Member can check the record. That is exactly what the Minister said.
It was very soon after that that we lost hope that the Conservatives would be able to muster the critical distance from the nuclear industry which we had hoped they might muster given some of the promises they made when the Liberals were in office. We then launched our own inquiry. We have been to several cities across the country and hope to have a report very soon which will make very clear the view of the NDP on a wide variety of issues pertaining to the nuclear industry.
I would not be crazy about many of the activities in which these two Crown corporations are involved whether they were done by a publicly or privately-owned company. This may be only wishful thinking, but I hope that one of the by-products of this privatization would be that the Government of Canada and other Governments, to the extent that the nuclear industry is privatized-in this case these two mining corporations- might be able to feel less attached to the whole industry.
I do not have any grounds for that wish because, as the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) pointed out in such detail, the private corporations in this industry have basically been able to do whatever they wanted to over the years and to attain whatever public governmental support they happened to need, whether in the form of direct subsidies, price fixings through cartels, or whatever.

So certainly there is no basis in history for hoping that the private nuclear industry will be treated with any greater critical attention than was the public sector. In fact, just the opposite has been true. The private companies have been able to operate with even less attention. However, I am hoping that at some time, some Government of Canada will turn its attention to the nuclear industry in the way that we have been calling for for some time and that it may be freer to do that if, in the case of uranium mining, these companies are completely in the private sector.
There is absolutely no doubt that there is a need for a full scale inquiry into all aspects of the nuclear fuel cycle in Canada. This is something that the Conservatives promised time and time again but have not fulfilled. This inquiry should include questions of reactor safety, emergency planning and other post Chernobyl questions that have not been addressed.
The only place where any of the more difficult questions pertaining to the nuclear fuel cycle have been addressed is in some of the committees of the House. The Standing Committee on Environment and Forestry, largely at my own initiation some time ago, began a study of the disposal of high level radioactive waste. It published a very good report entitled The Eleventh Hour. I recommend it to all Members of the House who should be interested in this whole question of the disposal of high level radioactive waste.
As well, I notice that the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources is involved in a study of the economics of nuclear power. These matters are being discussed as a result of parliamentary reform because the committees have initiated these studies on their own. It is a credit to the reform that these things are happening, but we still have not seen the Progressive Conservative Party live up to its commitment to have a full scale inquiry into the nuclear fuel cycle in Canada. We will probably not see that inquiry as we enter the last stages of this Government.
If there is a shred of integrity left in the Government it will call an election before it attempts to implement the Canada-U.S. free trade agreement so that Canadians will have an opportunity to make some judgment on an agreement about which there was no intimation in the 1984 election. If the Government has any respect for democratic principles, there will be an election before that agreement happens.
Of course, this means that the Conservative Party will have gone through its four years in office without living up to its promise in 1984 to have an inquiry into the nuclear fuel cycle in Canada.
There are many other issues I could speak about, but it would require more time than I have available. I know that a Member from the Liberal Party wishes to speak and I hope that I will be able to entertain some questions.

when it comes to the production of electric energy. Every province is committed to its own strategy for the production of electric energy. Madam Speaker, I want to begin by assuring members of the Government that we in the Official Opposition are not planning to protract this debate to any great extent. We have had two speakers and I have a few words to add. I do not think I will take even my full 20 minutes. I will, of course, be happy to participate in the question period, then we will be happy to see this Bill, which we generally support, move ahead.
I want to indicate, however, that 1 have very grave reservations about the Government's privatization policy as a whole. I was intrigued by the question asked by the Hon. Member for Edmonton Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie). He asked what it was that the Government has privatized that should not have been, and what has not been privatized by former Governments or by New Democratic Governments which should have been? It is an interesting question.
I think it is very easy to characterize the position of this Government. It has a very limited view of public purpose, even in Government itself, let alone in Crown corporations. It is slavishly addicted to the market-place in the belief that the solutions the market-place provides are always right. Indeed, underlying the free trade agreement is the idea that if only the provincial governments of Canada can be forced to live with market rules, without the power to mitigate them in anyway, that somehow or other it will produce a better life for Canadians. It may certainly produce some greater efficiency. I am not challenging that. I think the great thing the market does provide is a discipline about production. However, there is more to life than that. There is even more to business than that.
I think that if the Government has made an error in its privatization approach, it is the error of thinking that no matter what it is, the market-place will do it better than planning by Government or planning by others to try to achieve other objectives than just the efficiency for which market operations are quite rightly famous. We in the Official Opposition feel it is wrong to begin with the ideology that everything should be privatized. We have objected to the privatization of certain aspects of Correctional Service Canada. We have objected to some other privatizations the Government has proposed.
For us it is a practical question. The question has to be to look at the Crown corporation and ask if there is a public purpose for it that cannot be achieved or that will be lost if the

April 11, 1988
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
corporation is privatized? When the Government asks that question, and it looks at Crown corporation after Crown corporation, it will tend to come to the conclusion that they should be privatized, because the Government does not have a public policy purpose for Crown corporations.
For example, we have a business in Petro-Canada, but it is also a business that was established by Government to achieve a certain public purpose in addition to complying with the market-place, to being efficient and to providing a service like the service provided to the public sector. We wanted Petro-Canada to be a force in the operations of a number of private companies, which certainly operating together do not follow the typical or theoretical rules of the market-place because they are few in number, they are huge and are in fact a classical oligopoly. We wanted Petro-Canada to be out there, to be, among other things, the honest broker in the field, the corporation that would set the standard and compensate for the limitations that existed in that particular sector of our economy where so few companies together handle such an enormous volume of business.
De Havilland was another example of a corporation which was privatized. I have to say that I think the discipline of the market-place will help de Havilland. It has already begun to help. But when de Havilland was held by the Government it had a public purpose objective as well. That public purpose objective is lost now that it is owned even by a very good multinational corporation which is based and directed from the United States. The public objective which was lost was having a domestic indigenous aerospace industry in Canada, run by Canadians and achieving national objectives in its operation.
No one can say that however successful de Havilland is from now on-and I am one of those who want it to be successful and who support it-it will ever achieve that public policy objective that we had in mind when it was held in the public sector and which might have been achieved in the private sector if it had been sold to a Canadian control group.
The Eldorado Corporation is about to be put into the private sector. I think the role it has played over the years when it was in public hands justified, to a certain point, keeping it in public hands, but, as I have indicated, our energy critic and our caucus have examined the proposal and we consider it to be a proper evolution of Eldorado Corporation.
At the same time I have to say that we are very disappointed that the environmental problems caused by the use, production, exploration, or mining of uranium have not been satisfactorily addressed by the Government. We had looked forward to a continuation of work in trying to find methods of dealing with nuclear wastes that had not been found to date. We had hoped that that would continue to be a high priority.
There is nothing in this proposal to indicate that that will be a high priority and that any more than the normal concern of a private corporation will be shown to a problem of national
importance and one which would have benefited from continuing high profile responsibility in the hands of the federal Government.
Like some of the others for which this Government has been responsible, we fear that this privatization is more ideology than a practical consideration of the best interests of the Canadian economy and the best interests of the corporation being privatized.
When privatization occurs, it gives the Conservative Government the opportunity to turn to its friends and give them contracts to bring them on board into the operation. I do not have to be more specific in reminding this House that the Government has abused privatization in the past as a way of rewarding friends and giving them opportunities which would not otherwise be available.
One of the other motives of privatization, which is not a legitimate motive, and which the Government has used in the past, is the use of privatization as a way of appearing to reduce the size of the Public Service. Technically, the size of the Public Service or those employed in the public sector are reduced when a Crown corporation is sold or when a government operation is privatized. Unless there is an actual reduction in that activity, I do not think the Government is justified in claiming the credit for honouring its campaign promise to reduce the size of the Public Service.
The most scandalous example of this is what the Government has done in Correctional Service Canada where people who were working in the service as parole administrators or people in charge of half-way houses owned by the Government have been fired and rehired by organizations established through public funding purportedly to continue the same type of service, but in some cases in a less effective and efficient manner than was being done while the operation was entirely within the Government.
In a case like that, what is achieved is not a cost saving or a reduction in the number of people who are being paid for their services out of tax money, but the appearance that the Public Service has been reduced in numbers because those who were formerly in the Public Service are now under contract to the Government directly or indirectly and doing exactly the same thing. Privatization has become a pretty shabby business in the hands of the Government.
In conclusion, I simply express the hope that that will not be the case in this privatization, in this merger, and in the underwritings and the share offerings that will subsequently take place, but that it will be run on an above-board basis, and that in the long term it will bring benefits to the users of nuclear fuel and to the production of nuclear fuel.

I consider that to be a good insurance policy for the corporation. After all, a one-product company is as vulnerable as that product. While de Havilland's current plane is a very big winner or a very big success, in due course it will start to become obsolete. I hope that that is a long way down the road, but when that time comes I think the union and the Member of Parliament representing the area, myself, will be very happy that the company has other lines of activity which provide high paying jobs for very highly trained people who work in the plant.
I am not sorry that it has gone into the assembly business to the extent that it has, and I am not sorry that it is more than just a one-product plant. However, there is something discouraging, I must say, about making parts which fit into somebody else's aerospace vision or into planes being designed, assembled, and flown out of other factories than the ones de Havilland has in Canada.
I remember visiting other aircraft plants in that area of Toronto which were making tail assemblies, for example. That was the whole thing the company was about or the plant was involved in. One had to be somewhat saddened that the Canadian aerospace industry had the type of truncation that it would not be doing something where creative energy or vision or research and development could enhance what it was doing. It was just making as many tails as were needed for planes which had been designed elsewhere and which were being sold and marketed elsewhere, and so on.
That is the danger of the Mulroney trade deal. It is the kind of thing that we can see happening to our plants. As the takeover of American companies continues-and the agreement encourages takeover by American companies-it could lead to a lack of autonomy about Canadian entrepreneurship, Canadian economic creativity and invention, and so on. It is a very discouraging possible result of continentalism.
As long as the plant is designing planes and making them more or less from beginning to end, and as long as there is no suggestion that it will stop doing that, I will continue to support what is happening at de Havilland. As the Dash-8 meets its market and as new designs and so on come on, I hope they will come from de Havilland, not that de Havilland will merely be a piece maker for someone else's ideas.

Madam Speaker, it is interesting that we should come back after the break to yet another sign that the Conservative Government continues to pursue its ideological course toward defeat.
The interesting question which arises when one starts to discuss privatization and public ownership is in fact the one which the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) raised some time ago-which kinds of companies, which sorts of enterprises would one want to see as private sector enterprises, and for what reasons would one want to see them in the public sector?
As a country we have had to make such choices on many different occasions throughout history. Ironically, earlier Conservative Governments often made the choice to put a company into the public sector for specific and important national reasons. It is for that reason that I find it especially unfortunate that the Conservative Government has taken an entirely ideological approach to reduce, for the sake of doing so, the number of companies held by the public as opposed to those in the private sector.
What is also interesting is that the approach it has taken in this area, as in so many areas, has been one of ideologically based nibbles. Yet it refuses to stand up forthrightly and take a position that reflects what it actually believes in terms of significant, large public enterprises, such as Air Canada, Petro-Canada, Canadian National, and CBC. There has not been any effort, despite ideological small harassments, to move against significant public enterprises, because it is so clear that public opinion is in favour of keeping public enterprises such as Air Canada, CBC, CN, and Petro-Canada in the public sector to ensure that they continue to serve the public as they have done in the past. Still, steps have been taken such as this one in
respect of Eldorado and a series of earlier smaller steps in respect of other companies in the public sector.
If one had a philosophy respecting the public sector of trying to assess which firms should be in and which should be out, it seems to me-and perhaps this is the last point I will make before the luncheon break-that a company with so much associated with it in terms of safety, in terms of environmental concerns, and in terms of the tremendous contribution of the Government to setting it up in the first place, is the kind of firm which one would inevitably say must be within the public sector.
May I call it one o'clock, Madam Speaker.

subtopic: ELDORADO NUCLEAR LIMITED REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I can pursue this point somewhat further, of all the companies which one might choose, a company which is dealing with nuclear matters is a company which should be under the most careful, most controlled scrutiny from the Government. A company which has received, as Eldorado Nuclear has, the tremendous support of government in assistance, both with respect to capital, development and marketing, through the cartel arrangements which have been discussed back and forth, that too is surely a company which should be kept within the public sector as something which the Canadian people have built and something from which the Canadian people should receive the returns.
Finally, of course, it is a company which potentially has an environmental impact that is frankly dangerous, that can damage communities and hurt workers. That too, is a company which has to be kept within the context of community ownership rather than allowed to go to the private sector where it will not have to face the same kind of responsibility to the community as a whole.
I think on that basis it is very curious that one would find this company chosen as a company to privatize. I think there are other considerations which also make it very difficult to justify the sale of this company to the private sector. One of those considerations is the simple fact that the workers, who work not just those for Eldorado but for the sister company, which will be joining it as part of the scheme, have come out absolutely and adamantly against putting this enterprise in the private sector. They have done so for the best of reasons; for reasons of health and safety for themselves as workers and for future workers as well. They have pointed to the fact that up until recently statistics have shown that for those who are within such plants as the processing plants of Eldorado Nuclear, those who are actually mining uranium, the rates of danger with respect to cancer and with respect to other
April 11, 1988

consequences of radiation are significantly greater than for any other group within the economy.
So I think it is an important consideration in our decision making with respect to this privatization that we take into account that those who belong to both trade unions, the group which come from the United Steelworkers and the group which come from the energy and chemical workers, have adamantly opposed this privatization.
I think it is crucial for us to recognize that this is a tremendous sweetheart deal being offered to the private sector. There is, for instance, with respect to environmental considerations, the fact that the refinery at Port Hope essentially will be bailed out by the federal Government. With respect to the costs of dealing with that dumpsite, only the first $2 million worth of costs will be covered by the newly privatized company. For the next $98 million worth of potential problems, 76.5 per cent will be covered by the federal Government. Anything which is above that $100 million mark will be borne by the federal Government entirely. That is not the reality of private enterprise with its risks and its uncertainties. That is instead a kind of public enterprise which is really being handed to a small group of people who will receive shares in this newly privatized company.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Bill 2, tabled in the Saskatchewan Legislature last week, is a suppression of existing rights in favour of the French-speaking minority in Saskatchewan. The action of the Devine Government must be viewed as a backward step in terms of national unity. The Saskatchewan legislation runs directly counter to and contravenes the fundamental purpose of the Constitution of Canada which, after all, is to protect the basic rights of all Canadians.
Last week the Prime Minister wrote the Premier a somewhat ambiguous letter in which he said to the Premier of Saskatchewan that the Bill can be viewed from two different perspectives. He said it can be seen as open and generous because it implements long neglected rights and guarantees.
April 11, 1988

But he said, on the other hand, that the Bill can be seen as diminishing existing language rights.
What exactly is the position of the Prime Minister of Canada? Would he clear up some of the ambiguity in his letter and tell us whether he supports the Saskatchewan legislation or not?

subtopic: NATIONAL UNITY-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: NATIONAL UNITY-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out to the Prime Minister that the comparison with Ontario is not correct. As far as I know, there was no law in Ontario that for 83 years guaranteed access to the legislature or the courts.
In Saskatchewan, such a law existed, and that is the point. In Saskatchewan, there is a clear-cut loss of rights, and that is why we are raising the issue.
Perhaps I may remind the Prime Minister of what he said in this House on October 6, 1983.
He said, among other things, that the House has a duty to protect language minorities wherever they may be, because, and I quote:
There is only the sanctity of minority rights. There is no obligation more
compelling and no duty more irresistible in Canada than to ensure that our
minorities, linguistic and otherwise, live at all times in conditions of fairness
and justice.
My question to the Prime Minister is this: How can he reconcile what he said at the time with the action taken by the Saskatchewan legislature with Bill 2, which abolishes Francophone rights recognized since 1905 when the province was created? How does he reconcile this with a decision that is regressive and extremely damaging to our national unity?

subtopic: NATIONAL UNITY-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not expect to reconcile positions that are sometimes totally divergent. One hundred and twenty years ago, Canada's Prime Minister had to deal with problems on the language front. That is still the case today, and I assume it will be a hundred years from now. It is part of the very nature of our federation. Language problems will always be there to upset us, to trouble us and also to divide us. We must show maturity, leadership and generosity in dealing with these issues, and that is what we want to do. That has been, I believe, the admirable attitude of the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier since he became a Member of this House. I think that has been the position taken by the Leaders of the three political parties in this House, and we intend to maintain the same maturity and dignity in dealing with difficult problems.
We have a problem today, I agree. We will have problems five, ten and fifty years from now. However, there will always be people with the leadership and the resolve to deal with these questions in the appropriate manner, and I can assure the Hon. Member of my Government's clear commitment in this respect.

rights in their broadest context, so as to build on the achievements of the
Constitution Act of 1982 and the 1987 Constitutional Accord.
There is only one way to protect minority rights in this country, Mr. Speaker, and that is to entrench them in the Constitution. We had a chance in 1982 to do it perfectly, and we failed to do it perfectly. But we have built on it, and there were improvements.
In fact my hon. friend, who is perfectly consistent on this very important matter, as I recollect voted against the 1982 Constitution Accord because it failed to protect Frenchspeaking minority rights in the Province of Ontario. He has been perfectly consistent throughout the piece.
Improvements were made in 1982. Improvements are being made in 1987. But there is only ultimately one way to ensure the sanctity and the irreversible nature of the protection of minority rights and that is to have them in the Constitution. That is the commitment of this Government. That is what we have been working toward. Tomorrow we maintain the dialogue with the Province of Saskatchewan in a sensitive and important area to make progress on behalf of a Frenchspeaking minority in the Province of Saskatchewan.
The Premier of Saskatchewan has indicated, and if I may say to his credit, a degree of openness that he has put on the record that is encouraging, and to which we ought to respond in a mature and thoughtful way.
On behalf of the Government of Canada I propose to engage in that dialogue, with a view to providing excellent protection for our French-speaking minorities in Saskatchewan and elsewhere, for language minorities across the country, Englishspeaking and French-speaking. That is in the traditions of this House, that is what all Members seek, and that is to what this Government is committed.

That is the purpose of the policy we are following: it is a policy direction that is looking forward, past the next week or two, and I would appreciate it if the Hon. Member would cast his mind past the next week or two to understand the implications of what we are trying to achieve.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to return to the key theme I wanted to put before the House this morning with reference to this Bill, that is, that the Government has not thought through, in any sort of systematic way, which companies should be in the private sector and which companies should be in the public sector. What justifies Air Canada, Petro-Canada, and various other such companies being in the public sector and what justifies putting other companies such as de Havilland and Canadair into the private sector?
1 do not believe that the Government has logically and sensibly analysed the public purposes of a given company or the particular nature of that company's activities, but rather has casually looked at the public opinion polls and seen that the Canadian people support keeping such companies as Air Canada, Petro-Canada, and CN in the public sector. Other companies of which the Canadian people are not as aware are potential victims for what is in effect an ideological commitment to transferring companies out of the public sector just for the sake of doing so.
That is in fact what has happened. It has already cost us some significant possibilities for the future of the country. For example, in our aircraft industry we had the possibility, with Canadair and de Havilland, of creating an aerospace industry controlled and owned by Canadians which would contribute to a high-tech future in our industrial sector. Instead, we split these two companies and privatized them. The consequence has been, as was noted by one of the Members who spoke this

April 1 1, 1988
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
morning, that de Havilland is now more and more producing parts of Boeing aircraft for someone else rather than aircraft designed by Canadians creating jobs here of a high class for designers and producers, which would give the country a sense of export potential as well.
In the case of Eldorado Nuclear and the mine which is being privatized at the same time by the Saskatchewan Government I see the same kind of ideological thinking that lies behind what this Government has done so far. It is an ideological thinking that simply does not carry with it a logical, analytical point of view which looks at the nature of the companies themselves.
I said this morning, and stress again at this time, that when you are talking about an industry, such as the nuclear industry which has serious health concerns and serious consequences for the environment, like uranium mining and uranium refining, an industry on which we in this country have decided to take the military policy of not allowing our uranium to be used for military purposes-when you have an industry as unique as that, as clearly tied up with public purposes as that, that is precisely the sort of industry that we should keep in the public sector, because of these considerations.
I urge the Government to seriously reconsider its decision to privatize this company. I believe the deal it has made is financially very poor and risky.

As was indicated in an excellent article in the The Globe and Mail, the truth is that Mr. Roman's uranium empire was founded on no-risk, guaranteed cost-plus government weapons contracts. His empire would not have survived its first 20 years

That is precisely the kind of crucial public industry serving a public purpose which should be within the public sector. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the points that I made with respect to how one distinguishes between a firm that makes sense as a public sector firm and one that makes sense as a private sector firm answers that question.
When one considers the environmental dangers associated with uranium mining and uranium refining, one could not associate them with automotive production any place in this country. Radiation hazards from Chrysler Corporation's activities do not exist in my constituency. They do exist from a nuclear reactor which sits just across the border. That has much more potential danger for my constituents than would be the case with the automobile industry.
If we take the question of the massive subsidies and cost guarantees which were given to the uranium industry, which I outlined in answer to the last question, that too is something which cannot be associated to nearly the same extent with the automotive industry.
It is true that loan guarantees have been provided to Chrysler Corporation in my constituency. Frankly, my position
April 11, 1988

would be that if Parliament decided to provide money in the form of a large scale grant to Chrysler Corporation, as was the case with Ford's engine plant in my constituency, the Government should have some return in the form of equity investment to make a response for that particular contribution. However, that is not the case which was made with respect to Chrysler Corporation.
Finally, if we take the question of worker health and safety, it is quite clear that from the point of health and safety, the workers in this uranium industry are much more at risk. They are much more at risk because of the radiation factor and the whole nuclear connection that that implies than is the case with the workers of the automotive firms to which my friend referred. So I do not think any of those factors follow.

subtopic: ELDORADO NUCLEAR LIMITED REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I take pleasure in participating in this debate, but I must say I have a real problem with Bill C-121 which intends the sale of Eldorado Nuclear and the merger with the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation. I see heavy public subsidies being paid out in order to minimize the risk for the private sector.
I have been thinking about this question of privatization. One of the question asked by the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) was if there were any circumstances in which the sale of a Crown corporation could be acceptable and would make sense to New Democrats. The answer, of course, is yes. As my colleague, the Hon. Member Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), said this morning, the sale of Flyer Industries by the Manitoba Government, for example, which is currently underway, is a sale which, in this case, has been compelled, if nothing else, by market conditions and by a reluctance on the part of other provincial Governments involved in the transportation field to make it possible for Flyer to continue to prosper as a publicly-owned concern, and there may be other reasons as well.
What we are faced with is not a group of decisions about which is the best way to carry out certain objects of public policy. It seems to me, if we judge questions of industrial development where Government is involved according to that yardstick, there would be certain cases where it makes sense to use the public centre to create or expand a Crown corporation to achieve a particular public goal. In other cases, it would make sense to have mixed enterprise, some kind of joint venture or co-operative venture or some kind of sharing between the public and the private sector. In other cases, it makes more sense to leave a particular enterprise or industrial initiative in the hands of the private sector without public involvement, or with very loose public involvement.
I think most Canadians would agree that to talk in those terms is quite reasonable. They support public enterprise with such very substantial and important corporations as Canadian National, Air Canada or Petro-Canada. These are part of our
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
daily lives as Canadians. They help to knit the country together. They carry out important mandates on behalf of the people of Canada and help to maintain Canadian control in important industries such as the energy sector.
The bulk of Canadians believe these Crown corporations should remain in public hands. I think what Canadians as a whole resent, and what people I talk to resent, is the ideological approach taken. Dare I say it? If we were ideological about it, the New Democrats might be criticized on this particular question. Certainly, the Progressive Conservatives are criticized on this particular point.
Since coming to office the Government has taken the view that the private sector is by its nature good and should be supported and encouraged, and that the public sector is by its nature bad and should be discouraged. Therefore, what we are seeing is a kind of one-way flow of publicly owned Crown corporations sold off by the Conservative Government. Many have been sold at great cost to the taxpayers. We know about de Havilland and the amounts of subsidies involved there. Boeing was virtually paid to take de Havilland off the hands of the Canadian public. There was the sale of Canadian Arsenals, the sale of Teleglobe Canada under somewhat questionable circumstances, the sale of Canadair and so on.
There has been a whole series of sales. But somehow, according to this Government, there are never any important initiatives which need to be taken in which the public sector perhaps needs to be involved or if the public sector does need to be involved, there are grants, tax subsidies, concessions and contracts, that kind of thing. But these are all maintained at arm's length. When we have suggested, for example, there should be public equity in return for tax concessions or other subsidies given to the private sector, we have had scorn heaped upon us for being socialists who would bring down the fabric and structure of the enterprise system in Canada. Of course, that is absurd.
If we look to the south, to the United States, the home of free enterprise, we find that the degree of subsidization and public involvement in the private sector is, of course, even greater than it is here, particularly through its Department of National Defence. The Americans have used all kinds of tricks and devices in order to, shall we say, make private enterprise look good. I would suggest that that is not a particularly good policy to offer here.
I suggest there are reasons why Canada is somewhat different from the United States and that those reasons justify the use of public enterprise in some cases, they justify the use of mixed enterprise in some cases and they justify private enterprise in many cases, because the market can be an effective means of allocating resources. It certainly is an effective means of decentralizing decision-making. One can argue with some justice that the Government cannot make all the decisions all at the same time. When it tries to do so, it finds itself in situations which can be counterproductive.

April 11, 1988
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
Let me come back to this particular suggestion of privatizing Eldorado Nuclear. My colleagues who have spoken on this issue have already indicated our reservations. They have indicated the reasons for our opposition to Bill C-121, beginning with the fact that it is a bad deal. The Government of Canada is forgiving close to $600 million in loans.
There are advances which have been made to Eldorado Nuclear. In addition, it is taking on the lion's share of any environmental risks from clean-up of the Port Hope refinery. A sum of $75 million is specified and it could go much higher than that if the cost of clean-up exceeds $100 million. On top of that, there is no indication at this time of just what the share flotation of Eldorado Nuclear, or this merged company, will yield as far as the Canadian taxpayer is concerned.
1 would suggest that if we judge this deal on pure private sector criteria it would in fact be found wanting. The uranium markets in North America right now are depressed. The price is low. Unlike Denison Mines, the two companies in Saskatchewan do not have the benefit of sweetheart contracts with Ontario Hydro to carry them through rough times. Even though the oil reserves of the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation are relatively low cost to produce, it is not a good time to be looking for substantial profits in this particular industry. The future prospect is not a heck of a lot better, I suppose, because there are questions being raised about nuclear power. The number of new nuclear power stations is very limited, so that the future demand for uranium will no longer grow at the rate anticipated in the 1970s when Ontario Hydro entered into that very rich contract to which I have just referred.
If this was Canada incorporated, a conglomerate which ran a whole range of enterprises, as in effect the Government of Canada does, and it was decided to prune in certain areas in order to augment activities in other areas, there would be real questions about selling at the bottom of the uranium market, which is essentially what is being done in disposing of Eldorado Nuclear at this particular point in time.
On top of that, there is the question of the responsibilities of a responsible shareholder, in this case the Government of Canada. Are there other reasons besides profit which induced the Canadian taxpayer to take over Eldorado during the Second World War? The answer, of course, is that there certainly were. At that time it was a new technology. It was connected with the atom bomb. At that time there were concerns, which persist to this day, about the health and safety of workers exposed to radioactive substances. Today we know a lot more about the incredible problems with respect to the disposal of nuclear wastes, refinery tailings and so on.
I am not satisfied that in privatizing Eldorado Nuclear we are seeing a situation in which the taxpayers are going to see those risks privatized. If they do see those risks privatized then it may be at the expense of the workers involved. We do not know what the situation will be for them. All of the honeyed words of the former Minister of State for Privatization have
not convinced me that the jobs that will be affected will be secure, something which she tried to tell the House before this debate was adjourned prior to the Easter break.
If there are undue risks to be borne by the workers, then I have questions about that. I believe that the nuclear industry is a particularly sensitive industry. If there are risks to be assumed which will be borne by the taxpayers, then I want to know what those risks will be. What this really means is that there is a great deal of cosmetics used in order to try to make this sale look good and in order to get the company out of public hands. For what reasons? As I stated a few moments ago, it is for ideological reasons.
When the debate began I was reminded of the way the country developed. It is amazing that there has been a great deal of public intervention in Canada's economy since the foundation of our country. We have to ask why that has been the case over the course of so many years. Perhaps it is because it is something which is unique to Canadians. Perhaps it is also related to the size of our country. We would not have a country stretching 3,500 miles east to west which has been as successful, significant and important as Canada has been next to our southern neighbour if we had not interfered with market forces that would have turned Canada into a series of economic colonies of the American regions to the south.
If most Canadians were asked whether they would be willing to become new Americans and perhaps see a 1 per cent, 2 per cent or 3 per cent increase in their standard of living as a consequence or whether they wanted to stay Canadians, you, Madam Speaker, know very well that their answer would be, "We wish to remain Canadians, thank you very much".
That is a strong feeling in the country. We are different in our way of doing things. One of the things that my good friend Herschel Hardin pointed out in his excellent book entitled A Nation Unaware: the Canadian Economic Culture is that Canada has a public enterprise culture. In other words, we have become quite good at using public enterprise as an instrument for national development. I suppose this came from the intendant Jean Talon who was the economic genius who helped to build the economy of New France back in the 17th century in and around what is now Quebec City. That was at a time when he worked as the Minister of Economic Affairs in conjunction with Bishop Laval. The Government of Canada assisted with the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway at that time in terms of land grants. That was a premature or primitive form of public intervention. However, it ensured a national railway for Canada without which we would not have a country today.
We pride ourselves today on the competitiveness and the productivity of our steel industry in Hamilton, Sault Ste. Marie and other parts of the country. It is forgotten by those private enterprise advocates who say that Stelco and Dofasco are fine instances of Canadian productivity compared with the
April 11, 1988

American steel industry that the Canadian steel industry was a wartime creation. It began life in the public sector. It was a force-fed type of economic development to give Canada a sufficient steel industry with which we could participate in the war effort during the Second World War. It is on that basis that we have an industry which has been in place for 45 or 50 years. It did not exist before that time. It would not exist had it not been for the initiative of the public sector.
Defenders of the market ignore the fact that there is intervention by any Government. The United States Government intervenes when the Senate brings in a Bill, as it just has, which will limit Canadian uranium exports and penalize American utilities which seek to use Canadian uranium as a source of energy.
The United States has a policy of intervention in the market when there is discrimination against competitively priced Canadian softwood being exported to that country. That country intervenes when it uses its countervailing procedures which are grossly unfair in order to force the price of Canadian potash above market levels and to bring them in line with the uneconomic prices of potash produced in mines in New Mexico. The American Government intervenes constantly in terms of the way in which it develops research and development contracts with the private sector for the development of weapons, something which is done in the public sector in other countries such as the United Kingdom, France and Israel.
It should not be said that there is no intervention. Almost any Government makes decisions about interest rates, credit policy, consumer protection, trade policy and tariffs. The list is endless. All of these measures represent intervention in the economy.
One form of public participation in the economy is through the use of public enterprise. There is nothing wrong with it. It is fair to add that it does not mean that it is necessarily justified in every case. As a New Democrat I believe that we should put a halt to the constant strain of piecemeal privatizations which are being brought about by a Government which somehow wants to prove to a few of its backers, such as Mr. Bulloch, the National Citizens' Coalition, the Fraser Institute and others, that it is living up to an agenda which was enforced under Ronald Reagan's Government. It has been enforced under Mrs. Thatcher's Government in Great Britain as well. It is something which has brought economic misery to large parts of Britain even today. It has not been demonstrably aided in terms of innovation and initiative in many cases. I believe it is blinkered and wrong, given the important role that public enterprise has played in Canadian and other foreign economies over many years. I do not believe that it has come to an end.
I think that when the NDP forms the Government we will have to look at the portfolio of enterprises that are in the public sector. We will have to decide that perhaps certain ones should be expanded, be given a new mandate and be allowed and encouraged to grow. Certain ones are extremely competitive and extremely effective. I refer to Air Canada. However,
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
some are short on equity investment because of a penny-pinching attitude on the part of the Government of Canada. That is because the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), his Minister responsible for privatization, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and other Members of his Cabinet have burned into their minds that private sector is good, public sector is bad. Therefore they want to demean a sector of the economy which is extremely important to many Canadians and which is the only way in many cases by which we can ensure that there is economic and social justice for large numbers of Canadians.
Today in the House of Commons I asked the Minister of Finance about the Government's policy concerning interest rates and exchange rates. They indicated that the Government wants to legislate for southern Ontario and ignore the problems that prevail in many parts of the country which do not have the buoyant economy of the area around Metropolitan Toronto. In Newfoundland there may be no other way to develop jobs and to develop enterprise except through the participation of the public sector. The provinces increasingly find, as do American states, that they have to be involved in different ways. This sometimes has to be through ownership, participation, subsidies and tax concessions.
What does it say to the people of Newfoundland if there is a Government which says, "Public sector is bad, private sector is good"? What it says is that appropriate solutions to the problems which are out there cannot be used.
That brings me back to the particular question with which we are dealing today. We think this is a bad deal. We think that the Government is paying excessively to try to make this particular deal look good. We think that the type of blank cheque that the nuclear industry as a whole has received from Government in terms of the risks that it may be forcing the Canadian public to bear is unacceptable. This is an example of how the Government intervenes in order to reduce the risk for the private sector so that it can then say, "Private sector is good, public sector is bad".
I do not want to pursue this matter too far. I find the whole tenor of thought excessively illogical and unacceptable. I fear that after this measure is passed we could see a monopoly develop, particularly if Denison Mines under its new chairman and chief executive officer bids for majority control. We could see a situation in which the United States Government decides to close the door to future exports of uranium from Canada. I would imagine that that would be a disaster for the uranium industry in Saskatchewan. I am not sure how this new corporation would be able to deal with that.
I wish to conclude by saying that there are implications for the workers which have not been met, there are implications for the environment, and there are implications in terms of future economic policies in this country, if we have a government that continues to blind itself to the fact that the public sector and public enterprise can do an effective job under

April 11, 1988
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
certain circumstances. They should not be categorically ruled out, which is the position taken by the Government. It is wrong to take that position.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I listened carefully to the comments of the Hon. Member who just spoke, and I wish he would explain.
