speechtext:
Madam Speaker, that is a good question. If we look at de Havilland, since we have no clues as yet how Canadair is going to operate, I must say the Government did not really pursue any of the alternatives. Member were responsible for a business he had acquired for practically nothing, although it had assets worth between $700 and $800 million, he could make a profit from privatization as well.

subtopic: ELDORADO NUCLEAR LIMITED REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
I wish to ask the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) a couple of questions. The Canada Development Investment Corporation was created by the former Government to market four Crown corporations: de Havilland, Canadair, Teleglobe, and Eldorado. There has been successful marketing of three of those corporations. De Havilland doubled employment and now has a list stretching into the 1990s for the sale of aircraft from that corporation. There is solid, first-class employment and excellent R and D; it is at the leading edge in short take-off and landing aircraft. Canadair with new contracts is indicating a new spark and go. That was a first-class privatization with the sale to Bombardier. Teleglobe has blossomed forth with a sale to Memotec. Now we have Eldorado and a situation where we want to wind up Canada Development Investment Corporation and we have a partner that has massive uranium resources, and we can combine that with the refining capacity of Eldorado.
I cannot understand why my friend would oppose that privatization or the winding down of corporations that not only
this Government but the prior Government felt were no longer needed or the ownership by Canada of which was no longer in the public interest. Here is an opportunity to complete what has been a program not only of this Government but of the prior Government.
It is a situation where we continue to own shares in the corporation, where we combine with a province and a provincial Crown corporation that itself wants to bring in outside capital. I wonder where the problem is. What is the hang-up? Is the hang-up the same hang-up the Hon. Member had on the de Havilland Bill, the Canadair Bill, and the Memotec sale? Is the hang-up not that the Hon. Member does not want us to get out of business, and that the Hon. Member wants these corporations?

subtopic: ELDORADO NUCLEAR LIMITED REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
I hear my colleague, the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs, the Hon. Member for Mississauga (Mr. Blenkarn), with whom I normally enjoy quite cordial relations, suggesting that the Government should get out of business. I guess what he means is that he wants the Government of Canada to sell off Air Canada, Canadian National, and Petro-Canada. I am not sure what else is on his list. The Hon. Member should reveal his shopping list. This is what is bothering me with respect to the question of Eldorado. The fit in terms of community of interest between Saskatchewan Mining and Eldorado is a natural one. I do not dispute that. But there is no particular reason why that could not have been explored in terms of the two companies working together or joining together and remaining under public ownership. But the Government intends to privatize them and sell them off.
In my speech I suggested that what is particularly objectionable is the fact that the Government is saying that it only has one solution to those questions, which is to privatize. Under no circumstances does it envisage a role for the public sector. That represents a very substantial and, I believe, undesirable turn of policy.

Madam Speaker, it is always a pleasure to participate in these debates, particularly after having listened to an argument between the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) and the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), accusing each other of being reactionaries on one side or another of an argument and discussing between them which one has the worst hang-ups either for or against public or private sector enterprise.
Of course the recipe is neither solely private enterprise, as the Conservatives would sometimes want us to believe, nor is it as simple as to say that if we socialize everything including the local hardware store it will solve all problems, the way New Democrats sometimes pretend it will. Life is a little more complicated than that.

April II, 1988
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
Our country has been a prosperous nation because it has sought and achieved a good balance between private and public sector involvement in various areas. Of course from time to time it becomes necessary to adjust the policy, acquiring things from the private sector and equally disposing of things to the private sector if and when particular endeavours no longer achieve a useful purpose.
We in the Liberal caucus are basically in favour of the principle of disposing of that particular asset, but we have some reservations. Of course we know that the assets of Eldorado are in the area of S915 million, while the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation has assets of some $973 million. In other words, both are roughly the same in terms of assets.
We are told that the corporation will have a 38.5 per cent share of the new company while Saskatchewan will have 61.5 per cent. Of course there are questions to be asked in that regard. One must ask why it is that the merger is, if not in the form of a gift, certainly a bargain basement opportunity for the Government of Saskatchewan. As I said previously, it does not mean that we are against the privatization endeavour per se. However, it would seem that the Government should at least do a better job in justifying the means and process used to arrive at the stated price.
I should like to refer to a press release dated February 2, 1988 which was entitled on one side "Canada" and on the other side "Saskatchewan". The press release speaks of the particular merger and future privatization of both uranium companies. It indicated:
"Both governments want individual Canadians to participate directly in the ownership of this world-class uranium mining company," said Mrs. McDougall.
It went on to indicate:
The new company we are creating will be fully privatized through a series of public share offerings. Precisely when all shares in the company are in the hands of the private investors will be determined by market conditions. But 100 per cent of the company will move from public to private ownership within seven years.
The next sentence is a very important one:
At all times, the control of the new company will be in the hands of Canadians.
Just how can we be that sure? Of course we are sure that it will be in the hands of Canadians while we are divesting; that is rather obvious. I see the Hon. Member for Mississauga South waving a copy of the legislation. I know that it is covered in the Bill. I do not want unduly to agitate the Hon. Member, but I bring to his attention that we could very well see again the other partners signatory to the so-called trade deal upset by a legislative measure which, when passed in the House, could very well be seen by them-and I am speaking of the Reagan administration in the United States-as a measure which in their language, not mine, is unduly restrictive for them in terms of potential investment opportunities.
I am not saying that everyone in the United States will rush to buy shares in the particular endeavour. However, human nature being what it is, all we have to do is tell people that they cannot do something and suddenly it becomes almost a prize catch if one is able to get whatever is forbidden. The perception of the grass being greener on the other side of the fence on many occasions creates that particular circumstance.
Much has been said about the Bill in the House of Commons. Many Hon. Members have spoken on it. I do not intend to delay its passage but merely to reiterate some of the concerns already expressed by my colleagues in the House. Of course my comments will be of their usual brevity, which you have undoubtedly known before, Madam Speaker.
We are informed that the head office of Eldorado will be moved to Saskatchewan. As a Member of Parliament from an area which has been subjected to transfers of government staff from time to time, namely, the Ottawa area, I want the assurance-and I have not received such assurance-that the 50 or so employees at the present head office of Eldorado will be relocated appropriately. As a matter of fact, we are led to believe that they may very well end up without jobs. We want an assurance that those people will be treated properly. We should like to see them kept on and receive appropriate treatment in terms of relocation or, in the event that employees are not willing to relocate, given fair and just compensation packages, so that they do not receive the all too familiar public service treatment given by the Conservative administration to so many of my constituents and many other people in the national capital area and elsewhere who happened to be unfortunate enough to work in the Public Service at the time the Government was elected.
We all remember that when the Government was elected it said that it had no plans for lay-offs. As a matter of fact it said that those people who were saying that the Government wanted to lay off 15,000 per year were fear-mongers and so on.

Well, Madam Speaker, Canadians know better today. Indeed Canadians are aware that this Conservative Government has been laying off public servants since the 1984 election, notwithstanding the formal commitments and the promises made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when he was Leader of the Opposition.
Madam Speaker, the Leader of the Saskatchewan Liberal Party has also expressed concern about the possibility that a company or a group of individuals might buy shares up to the 25 per cent limit, and people are wondering why the Government chose the magic figure of 25 per cent. Would it be that a prospective buyer is prepared to acquire exactly 25 per cent of the shares, or was a more objective criterion used? Why not 10 per cent as in the case of a bank? Why not some other figure? The Government has yet to tell us exactly why it did favour this 25 per cent share-selling process.
April 11, 1988

The previous Minister said in the House of Commons that 25 per cent would enable an individual or a shareholder to guide the new corporation under certain circumstances. What does that mean, Madam Speaker? We are not sure. We really need clear statements from the Government why it has arrived at that particular figure and whether there is a potential buyer or buyers right now looking for that stated magic 25 per cent.
Having aired those concerns in the House today, I do not want to delay the passage of this Bill unduly. I want to reiterate the concerns expressed by my distinguished colleague, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan), who has been our lead spokesman on these issues, and an excellent lead spokesman he is, and I know, Madam Speaker, that you would want me to say that about the distinguished Member.
I will now conclude my remarks and hope that the Government will be able to answer not only the questions that I have raised in regard to this deal but also those expressed by the Member from Cape Breton-The Sydneys and other Members of Parliament during the last days of debate on this Bill.

Would the Hon. Member comment on that from an historical point of view? Perhaps he would be prepared to give us an idea of present Liberal Party thinking with respect to companies such as these which have been grouped together under CDIC?
Mir. Boudria: Madam Speaker, I am always pleased to see that the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) has heeded my request to ask questions in this debate. I
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
listened, as he did, to the remarks of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South. My interpretation of what he said was that CDIC's role was to get rid of Crown corporations. It could very well be that one of the functions would be to dispose of whatever Crown corporation does not fulfil a specific or necessary public sector interest or mandate. There are obviously government assets which from time to time have to be disposed of, not only Crown corporations but other things too. It is wrong to suggest that the only thing that we want from this organization is to get rid of everything so it can do itself in as quickly as possible. It is a little more complicated than that. Of course, I am sure that on many occasions, we have seen Crown corporations being either dismantled or sold off by this Government in a way which was not in the public interest at all.
Need I remind Canadians and indeed Members of the House of the means we initially tried to use to dispose of the Canadian Arsenals Company, for instance? Why did we use that particular mechanism of starting up the bidding process three, four or five times in order to try to get rid of it? Why did we offer no protection for the workers? We eventually had to fight on the floor of the House to gain protection for the workers.
It is true that a world-class organization purchased Canadian Arsenals, so I am not blaming the purchaser of that corporation, which in that case was SNC Engineering Company, but I am blaming the Government. It was the Government's job to look after its workers, but it failed to do so. The proof was in the pudding, because eventually the Government had to backtrack, change its mind and correct the mistakes it had made.
There is plenty of proof of the fact that the job of the Government and its agencies is not strictly to get rid of

subtopic: ELDORADO NUCLEAR LIMITED REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I am pleased to have a chance to say a few words on Bill C-121, an Act to authorize the reorganization and divestiture of Eldorado Nuclear Limited and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof. We are at second reading stage of this legislation, and therefore we are talking about the principle of the Bill.
Before I begin making some specific remarks on the principle of the Bill, I would like to reflect back on some past incidents. While government Members were in opposition, they promised the Canadian people on a number of occasions that they would conduct a royal commission into the nuclear industry. I recall the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and a whole host of cabinet Ministers and members of the government Party campaigning on this issue during the last federal election because of the interests Canadians have shown over the years in the existing state of the nuclear industry and the future of the nuclear industry in Canada.
Any Canadian who has given thought to this matter would say that there are still many unanswered questions about the nuclear industry. The future of the nuclear industry, not only in Canada but globally, is important for all of us. We were reminded of its importance by the Three Mile Island and the Chernobyl incidents. However, we have not seen that inquiry.
After three and a half years, there has been no indication whatsoever from the present Government that it plans to fulfil the promise it made to the people of Canada. When that became clear, the New Democratic Party decided to initiate its own inquiry into the nuclear industry. Some months ago, my colleague from Winnipeg-Birds Hill and my colleague from Vancouver-Kingsway decided to co-chair an initiative to look into this important matter, and they have been conducting a very intensive and extensive inquiry into the present state of the nuclear industry. They have held hearings in all parts of Canada including communities involved in the nuclear industry and those that are not. They are attempting in a most objective and open-minded way to welcome points of view on which to make a final recommendation prior to the next federal election.
Having said that, I want to go on record as saying that we are not enthusiastic about this particular initiative before us. It flies in the face of the promise for this important inquiry, and until we have some very clear answers about just what the future of the nuclear industry in Canada ought to be, I think it would be premature for us as New Democrats to support this initiative.
April 11, 1988

As a Member of Parliament who is from British Columbia, I remember not long ago when the Social Credit Government of British Columbia came up with what it thought was a brilliant idea. That idea was to form a corporation called BCRIC and to sell off a number of Crown corporations, providing shares for the general public to buy. As a matter of fact, it was such a good idea that the Government gave every resident of British Columbia five shares in BCRIC. This was to encourage all of us to become investors and, in theory, enterprising capitalists. It was to allow us to see how the stock market worked and to be a part of this new initiative by the Social Credit Government.
This little venture into popular free enterprise did not work very well. I remember the then Premier of British Columbia saying that he had confidence that the shares, which were trading at the outset at $5 or $6, would soon be trading at $12 and might go up as high as $20, and that this was a way for the young and old of British Columbia to understand the thrilling sensation of investing in the Vancouver Stock Exchange. Well, thrilling it was. It was a tragedy. I have not checked today but the other day BCRIC was trading at 91 cents, and my hon. friend from Mississauga tells me that it may be 90 cents today.
That means that all those folks who listened to the Premier of the day on this magnificent venture into the free enterprise system lost their shirts, and I suspect some even lost their undershirts, because they took the Premier at his word. In our system I guess that is not an uncommon thing for people to do, but they certainly found out very quickly that it was not good advice to invest in BCRIC shares.
As a Member of Parliament from British Columbia I recall those days with less than enthusiasm, and here we are once again, through this legislation, attempting to reorganize an industry and turn it over to the private sector and perhaps sell shares. That makes one extremely nervous.
I also want to pursue this in terms of the principle of selling off government assets. This is, of course, not any government asset. It is an asset within a very critical, important, and sensitive industry which concerns many Canadians. It is very critical in terms of our future planning in both a positive and negative way.
It is important that parliamentarians recognize that from the very beginning the private and public sectors in Canada have worked co-operatively. The establishment of the first settlements in Canada involved the Government of the day giving monopolies and contracts to various companies to build bridges, wharfs, rail systems, ports, and so on. That resulted in a marriage between the private and public sectors which, most of the time over the years, has worked relatively well. Canadians find it comforting.
I think of the economic activity which has taken place in my community of Kamloops in the last number of years since I
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
became a parliamentarian. Although unemployment has been a major problem which has plagued our area, I recall the development of a new armoury and a new airport, the upgrading of another airport, the establishment of some wharfs, community centres, highways, youth treatment centres, jails, young offenders' institutions, and lottery buildings.
I could continue for a long time making specific references to all sorts of government-initiated ventures which, with very few exceptions, were turned over to the private sector for construction. This has made a great difference in our community in the last number of years. Without these government-sponsored projects from the federal and provincial Governments there would be a significant increase in the already tragically high levels of unemployment. I simply point that out as an example of how government, industry, and business can work in a most productive and positive way.
I think it is fundamental that if one evaluates the sale of Eldorado carefully one will see that it is a bad deal. It is just not a very intelligent business arrangement. Therefore, we in the New Democratic Party oppose the deal in its present form for the simple reason that it is a bad one. It is bad because the deal is structured in such a way that the public sector takes the risks and obligations and the private sector gets the profits, not only from the commercial activities of the company merged from Eldorado and the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation but also from the heavy public subsidies which are given the uranium industry in the form of favourable taxation, marketing arrangements, and sweetheart contracts which I will comment on in a moment.
That is the bad deal. The private sector gets all of the goodies and the public sector, to be more specific the taxpayers of Canada, pick up the tab. I would say it is a good deal for the private sector, but for the taxpayers of Canada it leaves a great deal to be desired. That is why I wonder if some of my Conservative friends see this as a good deal for the people of Canada in the short or long term.
It is discouraging that we have had no assurances from the Government that it recognizes the sacrifice of the public sector and the public interest in this deal. It is clear that this deal has been structured so that the Government can say that privatization works, just look at the share price. What the Government does not say is that in order for this stock flotation deal to succeed-and that is what it really is-the public sector will underwrite the risks by assuming the debt of Eldorado Nuclear and the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation, and the federal Government will assume the further liability of Eldorado's nuclear waste problems at Port Hope at a cost perhaps as high as $75 million. That is only a guess at this time, but that is all we can go on.
This take-back of debt has been described by the financial advisers to the Government, Burns Fry, as necessary for this flotation initiative. Eldorado's debts are substantial. If my memory serves me well, they are in the range of $550 million. The federal Government will receive from the newly-merged

April 11, 1988
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
company about $250 million, leaving $300 million which must be made up in the sale of shares in the new company before the Government breaks even on its debt obligation alone. This is to say nothing about the cumulative investment which has been made in Eldorado in the form of government equity.
Therefore, the Government needs a high share price or it will wind up with a brick in its hands, or something like BCRIC which started out at $5 and is presently trading at 91 cents. However, is there any certainty of a high price? The uranium markets are currently in a chronic over-supply situation and the prices are depressed. In the last number of days we have seen an initiative in the Congress of the United States which would make it very difficult to continue Canadian exports into the United States. If the United States markets were closed to foreign producers in response to the distress of its own domestic suppliers' conditions, we would be caught in a most chaotic situation. The trade deal which the Government has negotiated with the United States appears to be worthless in terms of enabling us to do anything about the congressional initiative which the Senate passed enthusiastically a few hours ago.
There is no certainty of a high share price. Since there are no guarantees that the federal Government will get its investment in Eldorado back, let alone cover the debts that Eldorado presently owes, what are the other advantages or disadvantages of this deal?
In light of the many questions which my colleagues have asked throughout the day I think it is fair to ask whether there are job guarantees for the employees. Not surprisingly, in the true fashion of the Government, there are no job guarantees. Rather, the opposite is the case as the Minister spoke of the rationalization of the two companies. You and I both know, Madam Speaker, that "rationalization" is a nice word for "lay-offs". When we say that we are going to rationalize a company, that an industry is being rationalized, or that there is rationalization going on in the textile industry, it means that hundreds, thousands, or tens of thousands of people will be laid off, that they will be jobless.
In terms of the trade deal, this has become a most popular word. Members indicate that there will be some rationalization going on. It has a positive context. Since we like to be rational, we assume that rationalization must be a very positive process. It is positive in some respects because rationalization usually means modernization and more competitive businesses. However, in human terms, which we tend to overlook in this place, it means a loss of jobs or the termination of a career in a particular industry or company.
In recognition of this euphemism, the former Minister has indicated that there are no guarantees. She essentially said that there would be job losses or lay-offs.
What is the future for the Port Hope refinery, a site which has no room for expansion at the moment? The future is not
particularly bright, since Eldorado already made one attempt to build a uranium refinery in Warman, Saskatchewan, in the late 1970s.
What about the research and development prospects? There are real prospects for change in the processing of uranium enrichment, using laser technology. This will require a substantial commitment to more research and development. Will the new company pursue this research and development or, given the relaxation of enrichment requirements for Canadian uranium exports, will Canada return to being an unprocessed resource exporter?
Most Members who have spoken against this legislation are concerned that Canada will increasingly become an exporter of the raw material as opposed to developing a more finished product. The trade agreement, which drops our requirement for processing exported ore, certainly does not bode well for the future.
The Government has taken action on a number of fronts toward privatization. While the Government wants to turn all kinds of publicly owned corporations over to the private sector, according to inquiries made by various newspapers and financial publications, there seems to be some variance between what the people of Canada want and what the Government intends to do.
For example, the Government has indicated that it would like to sell Air Canada to private interests. In my province, the latest Angus Reid poll indicates that 72 per cent believe that Air Canada is well run. More than half the people in British Columbia believe the Government should not sell Air Canada. We live in a country where the majority view should prevail or be equal. It seems that the people in my Province of British Columbia feel that Air Canada is well run and should not be sold.
In British Columbia, 64 per cent of the people believe that Petro-Canada is well run, and 55 per cent say that the Government should not consider selling it in any way.
Let us consider CBC, which often gets a great deal of response from my prairie colleagues in the House. In the Prairies, 66 per cent of the people believe that CBC is well run and that it should not be sold to the private sector. An even greater majority in other areas of the country are in favour of the CBC, Air Canada and Petro-Canada.
The majority of British Columbians feel that Canadian National is well run and should not be sold to private interests.
The one exception to Crown corporations which most people believe are well run, which will come as no surprise, is Canada Post. That is the Crown corporation that I do not believe any Canadian feels is well run.
The Government is continually manipulating and changing the mandate of this corporation. One of the reasons that I believe the postal corporation is not being run well is that the Government has singled out this Crown corporation that
April 11, 1988

touches the lives of every Canadian as the one which should make a profit. There is no suggestion that the Department of Immigration should make a profit, or that our hospitals, universities, or Armed Forces should make a profit. Yet when the Government decides that this one government service, which touches every family, whether urban or rural, rich or poor, should make a profit, it is not surprising that this Crown corporation is not running particularly well.
I do not support the Government's initiative with this Bill. In closing let me say that it is time that we send this matter to committee for closer examination. Hopefully we will be able to address such questions as why there are no job guarantees for the men and women who work for these companies. There are many questions that must be asked and perhaps the most appropriate place to ask them would be in committee at the end of this debate.

My question concerns the open-ended guarantees being given in this particular case. The Hon. Member will be aware that Eldorado has a dump site in Port Hope. There are problems in terms of the clean-up of that dump site and, according to the Library of Parliament research staff, there has been a suggestion that this could cost as much as $100 million. Only 25 per cent of that would be borne by the Government but if the costs rise above $100 million it would be borne entirely by the federal Government.
Last night on the news there were comments by representatives of Energy Probe relating to the total lack of liability in the nuclear power industry for any type of defects in nuclear power plants which might bring civil suits against the manufacturers.
What is the Hon. Member's opinion about privatizing a company while leaving the risk in public hands? The Government of Canada will get some $200 million in debt instruments from this newly merged company but will have a $75 million liability which could possibly escalate to double or triple that amount.
Does it makes sense effectively to privatize a company but not force the private owners to take the risks that I thought were part of the private sector? Should not the new privatized owners take all of the risks rather than dump some of them back on the federal Government?

Madam Speaker, that is a very interesting question. Why are the taxpayers of Canada expected to assume all of the risks while the private sector is the recipient of all the obvious gains? That is a fundamental question which has been asked by a number of Members participating in the debate today.
My colleague has raised an issue which I did not have time to discuss. It concerns the whole matter of liability with respect to the disposal and treatment of wastes. He indicated very accurately that the taxpayers of Canada must accept that responsibility as well as the cost. It is a very unfair and unjust business transaction which is very biased in favour of the
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
private interests. It places very little risk on the private interests and all of the risk and most of the financial liabilities on the taxpayers of Canada. That is essentially why we are opposing this legislation.
There is also the whole matter of safety in this particular industry, to which my hon. friend alluded in his question. As you are probably aware, Madam Speaker, every year at least a thousand workers, men and women, die on the job sites of this country, to say nothing of the tens of thousands who are injured and as a result of their injury often spend an entire lifetime off the job. A thousand people are actually killed on the job sites of our country each year. That is one of the reasons that two major groups involved in this particular transaction that we are discussing today, namely, the energy and chemical workers and the United Steel Workers, oppose this Bill. They feel that the industry is bad enough already and once it is turned over to private interests the pursuit of profit will be carried out with more zeal than ever at the expense of health and safety in the workplace.
That is not only occupational safety but environmental safety, in the broadest sense as well. They are very concerned that there are no safeguards, nor any particular attention given to this critical matter in Bill C-121. Not only do the taxpayers of Canada accept the brunt of the risk and the loss in terms of a safe financing of equity, but the men and women who work in these operations are also being placed at greater risk than ever before in what we already recognize as a highly risky industry.

Madam Speaker, I think, once again, people get caught up in the rhetoric of this place. What my friend from Edmonton has indicated is simply not accurate. What we have said on a number of occasions is that our plans are for the traditions of the Canadian economy to continue. That is why at the outset of my presentation I thought it was appropriate to indicate that we are a nation that is recognized as a country where the private and public sectors have worked amazingly well co-operatively together in terms of generating a relatively healthy economy.
When I think back to the number of times when Governments, not only the federal Government but the Government of the province of my hon. friend, found a critical industry or business that was not working well, that was in financial difficulty or was not serving the people well, they decided that rather than simply have profit guiding every decision, it was important that people be serviced by certain kinds of industry.
So the Province of Alberta saw the wisdom of buying Pacific Western Airlines and Alberta Telephone. I remember those debates because the people of Alberta were getting hosed by the private telephone system and were not being served well by the various feeder airlines. So the Government of Alberta, which was not an NDP Government but a Government which had some imagination and reflected the views of a New Democratic Party Government, decided to take Pacific Western Airlines into its own hands in order to provide better service for Albertans, which of course it did. It then took over the private telephone system. Because it was a monopoly and, therefore, there was no competition, it was a tragic situation in terms of services, particularly to rural Alberta. The Government then provided the necessary and appropriate telephone service to Albertans regardless of where they lived. That is the kind of spirit we have seen in the past.
I do not know how long it would take to go through hours and hours of examples where provincial Governments and federal Governments have witnessed a situation where the private sector was simply failing to deliver the services they felt their respective citizens deserved and took action. So when
my hon. friend asks if we would consider turning any of the Crown Corporations over to the private sector, I would say that this is something we would enjoy reviewing. We would look at the list and see as times changed that perhaps there should be some that should be brought in and some that should be left out.
What I am saying is that at a time when Canadians from one coast to the other are concerned about the future of the nuclear industry, and extremely troubled by the nuclear industry in its present form, I am particularly reminded of the Chernobyl incident. Canadians want to know the most appropriate way to proceed as a country. That is why government Members opposite promised an inquiry into this important matter, which they failed to do. It took the New Democrats to provide that initiative, thank goodness. The New Democratic Party of Canada held hearings across the country and received input into this appropriate area and it will come forward with recommendations. At that time, the Parliament of Canada, based on those thoughtful recommendations, can see how best to proceed with something like Eldorado Nuclear.

Madam Speaker, I welcome the chance to take part in the debate on this Bill and particularly on this issue in general. I want to start by saying that I am going to try to make a Conservative speech. I am going to elucidate some good, sound Conservative principles that one adheres to if one is a Conservative or if one is a so-called private enterpriser. One of the principles is that an investor is entitled to an opportunity to get a return on his investment. If he gets a return, fine, but if he does not, he takes his chances according to the free market forces. I am repeating what many of my colleagues opposite on the government side have said for yea these many years. That being the case, I submit to the House and to my good friends opposite that the public investor is just as entitled to an opportunity to get a return on an investment as any individual private investor.
We have made that point on many occasions in this House over the years. But this deal penalizes the public investor, the taxpayers of Canada, who put the hundreds of millions of investment dollars into the uranium industry, as well as lots of other industries in this country. In many instances they received a return on investment. I am sure that some of my colleagues may not be aware that, with all the difficulties that the CNR is having, over the last few years it has paid out a couple of hundred million dollars to the Government of Canada by way of dividends. That is appropriate. The public investor received some modest, to put it nicely, return on his investment.
This deal on Conservative grounds, grounds of the most solid Conservative philosophy, is a bad deal. In light of the so-called opportunities for the private sector in uranium mining, refining, processing, et cetera, taxpayer investors are not receiving the type of opportunity to which they are entitled.
April 11, 1988

They are not receiving it because of this legislation. The public investor is being denied that opportunity. Where are the Conservatives who talk about the rights of the investor and of the opportunity to which the investor is entitled?
With respect to the issue of uranium mining, refining and processing I readily admit that in my Party we have had agonizing debates on the subject for years. They have taken place in my province, British Columbia, Ontario and in the national Party. Of course there have been difficulties. However, we came to a conclusion in the Saskatchewan section of the New Democratic Party that in spite of the fact that we formed the government of the day in the province, which was in the mid-1970s, as Party policy there would be no new or additional mines or additions to the present ones. It was decided that as and when a mine that was in existence and operating was phased out because of the depletion of the ore body appropriate actions would be taken to fully compensate the communities and employees involved. That has been the policy of my Party in my province for the last number of years.
I appreciate that once an industry is established, and in this instance with public investment, and when there are trained employees and the community is built up it is not easy to say arbitrarily, "We are against uranium mining and we will stop it as of yesterday". That cannot be done. We think that we have worked out a way to do it.
With respect to some good, Conservative, hard-nosed foundation philosophy, whatever happened to the old private enterprise theory about those who invest taking the risks and dragging themselves up by the bootstraps? That philosophy dictates that one is on one's own and relies on market forces. One takes one's chances. Whatever happened to that philosophy? This deal and others that have been mooted hand the gravy over to the private sector and keep the risks and any potential damages in the hands of the Canadian taxpayer.
Surely that is some type of betrayal of the foundation of free enterprise Conservative principles. I will have my twentieth birthday in June, and I wish I were that young. In the years I have been here every time there were economic difficulties, who were the first ones to come to Ottawa with their hands out asking to be bailed out? When cattle prices went down to nothing, the big ranchers who talked to me about private enterprise and dragging themselves up by their own bootstraps, some of whom worked on land which their parents or grandparents stole from the Indians, were the first ones down here demanding national government assistance. By their own actions privatization Conservatives, the so-called private enterprisers, are freeloaders. The fact of the matter is that without public investment the private corporate sector does not and will not invest. What it wants is all the marbles. It wants a lead-pipe cinch.
If members of the private sector were made to go out to find their own uranium ore bodies, invest in them and take chances, then not a darn one would do it. If it were not for the hundreds of millions of dollars put in by the federal Government and
Senate and House of Commons Act
several provinces I doubt that there would be a uranium mine anywhere in the country right now. Now that the taxpayers have made that investment, built up those industries, communities and employees, to whom will the Government turn them over? It will turn them over to those who want to become private owners.
Where were they when the country needed them? There are some Conservative thinkers who would say that if there were ever a place for the complete public control and ownership of an industry it has to be in the uranium industry. As a signatory to the non-proliferation treaty we cannot allow this industry to drift into private hands and be left to the tender mercies of the guy who will do anything to make a buck, even if it meant selling the stuff to the IRA and the PLO.
It is my belief that the Government intends to weaken the powers of the Atomic Energy Control Board, to skirt around, if not ignore, our international obligations, and to fly in the face or what is unquestionably the will of most Canadians. This is not an industry that should be left in the hands of those who are more interested in making a buck than in treating people decently and giving public investors an opportunity to obtain a return and, most important, an extension of peacemaking and peacekeeping in the world.
I take it, Madam Speaker, that you want to call Private Members' Hour. I will be happy to resume my remarks when this Bill is brought before us again.

that Bill C-257, an Act to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act (independence of Parliament), be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Madam Speaker, I have introduced this Private Member's Bill as a result of a conversation I had with the Clerks at the Table in the House, and also with some of the legal people in the House of Commons. The intent of this Private Member's Bill is simply to clarify in order that I, as a Member of Parliament, and any other Member who is also a farmer, rancher, or from whatever particular background, would be eligible for any government programs that applied to that particular class.

April 11, 1988
Senate and House of Commons Act
In the past I understand that there has been some confusion as to whether Members of Parliament actually qualified for certain government programs.
Approximately two years ago there was a great drought in southern Saskatchewan, southern Alberta, and Manitoba. Although I was not in the area that was covered by this drought, I was advised that, 1 would not be eligible for this government program.
I consider myself to be a farmer. I can say with some certainty that I will be farming in five or ten years from now. I cannot say that I will be in the House of Commons in five or ten years from now, because like every other Member of Parliament I have to go through that process, get the nomination for my Party, and then stand in a general election.
In order to clarify this for other people who may be contemplating running for Parliament, it should be made very clear that if the Government does in fact put a special program in place that applies to farmers or ranchers, I or some other individual who may be a Member of the House of Commons or a member of the Senate would still qualify for that program.
I have discussed this issue at some length with other Members of Parliament. I have also discussed it at some length with constituents of mine. I have asked them their views on a government program that applied to all farmers, for example, and excluded Members of Parliament or the Senate who also happened to be farmers. Each time I asked that question I was assured by my constituents that they would view that as rather a silly regulation. They do not consider me to be any less a farmer because I am also a Member of Parliament.
At the present time I operate my farm with hired help and with some of the operations done by a custom operator. But I still operate the farm, I am entitled to a Wheat Board permit, and I still carry on the operation exactly as I did before I was elected to represent my constituency. That is simply the reason that I wished to have this Bill introduced. The Bill clearly sets that out.
The key area was in some of the interpretations of the word "contract" entered into. If I were taking part in a government contract or bidding on a government contract it would be much different from simply receiving a program that was put in place to assist all grain farmers or all cattle raisers who were having difficulty because of international markets or weather conditions. The wording was very clear and indicated that the purpose of this Bill was to remove any chance that there would be a conflict of interest for a Member of the House of Commons or a Member of the Senate.
As I mentioned earlier, this apparently has been subject to question in the past with government programs that applied to a class of agricultural producers when people who actually sat in the House of Commons were questioned as to their eligibility to take part in this government assistance program. My intention was to clarify this matter in order that there would be no doubt that any general government program that applied
to grain farmers, for example, would also apply to Members of the House of Commons or members of the Senate.
The present Section 20(1) wording did require some clarification. As I mentioned, it was in the definition and in the interpretation of the word "contract".
The new clause that I have suggested be inserted reads very clearly:
21. This Act does not extend to disqualify any person as a member of the House of Commons by reason of his being
(a)	a shareholder in any incorporated company having a contract or agreement with the Government of Canada, except any company that undertakes a contract for the building of any public work;
(b)	a person on whom the completion of any contract or agreement, expressed or implied, devolves by descent or limitation, or by marriage, or as devisee, legatee, executor or administrator, until twelve months have elapsed after the same has so devolved on him; or
(c)	a contractor for the loan of money or of securities for the payment of money to the Government of Canada under the authority of Parliament, after public competition, or respecting the purchase or payment of the public stock or debentures of Canada, on terms common to all person.
There was a similar clarification regarding the rights of Senators.
The intent of my Bill is very plain. I have discussed this with other Members of the House and with my constituents. There seems to me general agreement that, because the Member of Parliament is elected, he or she should be permitted to take part in any Government program that is put in place that affects that general class. In this case, the most recent program that we had last fall was the Special Canada Grains Program.
Members of this House, as do members of provincial legislatures, and members of rural, town, or city councils often have to absent themselves from a vote pertaining to any particular legislation that may be seen as beneficial to them. The same could be held in the House. If we were voting to make that particular payment as part of a national program, possibly Members could be considered in some conflict of interest if they were supporting the legislation either as a member of the Government or a member of one of the opposition Parties, and they could simply absent themselves from that vote.
I am sure that I and many other Members of this House were members of municipal governments. I was a mayor and a councillor of my town for many years before I came here. If there was any possibility of a conflict we would simply leave the room when this particular item was being discussed, particularly when it came to a vote. This is commonly done. For example, from time to time our town council used to tender for vehicles. One local automobile dealer was also a member of council and when a bid would be submitted to council by the head office of the company he represented, he would not be involved in making a decision on whether or not council would accept the contract. I am sure that the same has been done in other municipal, city, and town councils.
April 11, 1988

The purpose of the legislation is quite clear. I want to assure people who are contemplating running for office that that would not make them ineligible for programs. 1 can particularly speak about western agriculture with some authority. We must take advantage of various available programs, and even then it is very difficult to make ends meet. We are involved in a cost-price squeeze, a vice ever tightening. Until such time as sanity returns to the international market-place and we can once again look to it to provide us with income, it is incumbent upon Governments, particularly the federal Government, to provide some limited support to producers.
The wheat from my farm should be sold for the same price at the local elevator as that of everyone else. There is simply not enough there, so out of necessity we must look for a special government program such as the Special Canadian Grains Program or other programs which are funded jointly by producers through a levy and the federal Government. It is unfortunate that at present we must look to Government for a good portion of the money required to keep our operations viable.
I want to assure everybody who is running for office wherever they happen to be that if a government program were put in place that benefited their particular class of agriculture, they would be entitled to share in it without any problem whatsoever.
This is the reason I introduced this Private Member's Bill. I am looking forward to comments from other Members in the House to see whether or not they agree with me or whether they have other suggestions to put forward at this time.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to participate in second reading debate of Bill C-257 standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Gottselig).
A little later an amendment may be presented to the House suggesting that we refer the matter to a parliamentary committee and withdraw the actual Bill. I think that would probably be the best way, if such a motion is forthcoming a little later as I understand could be the case.
The suggestion of the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw is a good one in many respects. We do not want people in the agricultural community to be discouraged from running for public office. I certainly would not want that. I am not a farmer, but I represent a large and very fine agricultural riding. I could argue that it is the finest, of course. However, if some day my constituents wanted to present someone who was a farmer, I would not want the person to be unable to enjoy the privilege of running for public office for the mere reason that he is a farmer.
The present situation, as we know, does not preclude anyone in any occupation from seeking public office. However, as the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw quite rightly pointed out,
Senate and House of Commons Act
financial constraints on the agricultural community are such at present, particularly in the grains and oilseeds sectors, that it is necessary to seek government assistance because of international pressures on agricultural commodities, namely, the price war between the EEC and the United States of America. Actually it is a subsidy war in which they insist upon bombarding each other with tax dollars to try to regain what each one feels is his rightful share of the market.
In amending the present Senate and House of Commons Act we do not want to create a situation which would prevent contractors and so on from receiving what is normally known as contracts with the federal Government. I recognize that under the Hon. Member's Bill contracts for public works would still be excluded. Nevertheless, there are other kinds of contracts which could potentially be carried out by Members of Parliament or concerns in which Members of Parliament have a share if we pass the Bill as presented to us now.
The long and the short of it is that I support what the Hon. Member is trying to do. I support his initiative in trying to create a situation which will not unduly discriminate against people who work actively in the agricultural sector from seeking public office. In my opinion we need more people in the agricultural sector to sit in Parliament. We should not do anything or create any circumstance which would make it unduly difficult for them.
Having said that, I hope we receive an amendment a little later which will refer the subject matter to a parliamentary committee for action.
In retrospect perhaps it would have been better to have a motion before the House rather than a specific Bill. However, it does not matter at this point as long as the concern is aired in the House and is referred to a parliamentary committee. Some have suggested that perhaps the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedures should deal with the issue. Perhaps the committee charged with looking at the new conflict of interest Bill after it has been passed at second reading could also look at the topic. Many of the issues with which that parliamentary committee will deal concern the conflict of interest of not only cabinet Ministers, the Leader of the Opposition, and so on, but indeed every Member of the House and the other place. In my opinion it would be an appropriate occasion to discuss the issue at that point as well.
I am offering it in terms of a suggestion. I am not married to the principle that we should absolutely discuss it at the same time. However, my reason for raising it is that if we refer it to another parliamentary committee it could have a tendency to go on the back burner, whereas the conflict of interest Bill will probably be discussed in the very near future by a special legislative committee of the House. Therefore, that would enable us to discuss the topic, which the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw brought to our attention, in an expeditious manner to ensure that at the next election, whenever it comes, the potential problem could already be solved.

April 11, 1988
Senate and House of Commons Act

Madam Speaker, having said that, I would end my remarks by expressing general support for the measure introduced by the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Gottselig), but I hope the Bill will be withdrawn so that the issue raised by the Hon. Madam
Speaker, it is a pleasure to respond to this initiative by the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Gottselig) regarding some concerns that he has brought to our attention which I think are legitimate and appropriate. The essence of his Bill would remove any financial or perceived financial impediment that some people might see to their becoming candidates for elected office, in this case as Members of Parliament or, as the Bill also indicates, members of the Senate. That is really quite a statement because once you are in the Senate you are there for a long time. We are talking about people coming from agriculture who, I suppose, for the rest of their lives are subject to some concerns raised here by the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw.
On balance, I believe this is an appropriate initiative and as quickly as we can we ought to put it to the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure. As the previous speaker indicated, since we will be discussing conflict of interest legislation very soon this could possibly be a matter that could be referred to that legislative committee at the appropriate time.
There are concerns which the Hon. Member mentioned with which I agree. He spoke about his experience at the municipal level. I guess most of us have had similar types of experiences. Whenever a vote came up that was perceived to be an obvious conflict, one simply left the room or failed to vote and doing that seemed to take care of things. In my career as a municipal politician I feel it was a rather ineffectual exercise, being well aware of how much influence a single member could exert on his or her colleagues to achieve a particular outcome with or without that individual's participation in the final vote.
A recent initiative that has caused a great deal of concern is the allocation of northern benefits. We have some pretty peculiar parts of Canada that have been referred to now as northern areas which receive special tax consideration. On one side of the street in some communities you are eligible for northern benefits, but if you live on the other side of the street you are not. I suppose if Members of Parliament had an opportunity to determine whether northern benefit allowances for tax purposes should be associated with a particular area we might be inclined for rather obvious reasons to be supportive of some of these initiatives. As the Hon. Member has indicated in his Bill, particularly in the explanatory notes, he refers to
members of the class, such as farmers. The Member mentioned farmers, grain producers and ranchers.
We have various government programs to support the grain industry because of the international competition that is becoming more and more unfair as a result of increased subsidies from both the United States as well as the European Economic community. But we must think about parts of western Canada which this year will be experiencing severe drought problems unless there is quite a dramatic shift in traditional weather patterns. This would result in an initiative such as the Hon. Member is bringing to our attention and perhaps some Members of Parliament would be influenced in terms of their own ranches.
In principle, I am very supportive of the initiative and I want to thank the Hon. Member for bringing it forward. Let me say that in the appropriate committee when we come to examine the behaviour of Members of Parliament as to when they should or should not vote we ought to give that a great deal of consideration.
In conclusion, I do think that rather than proceed in the usual fashion when it comes to proceeding with Private Members' Bills that would be unnecessarily cumbersome, a more expeditious approach probably would be to refer at least the content of this Bill to the appropriate committee, which presumably would be the committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to tell the House that I am a farmer and I have owned a farm so I have a particular interest in the subject which the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Gottselig) has presented. I listened with interest to his speech and to the speeches of the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott- Russell (Mr. Boudria) and the Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap (Mr. Riis).
I appreciate the opportunity to participate in the debate of Bill C-257. As all Members are aware, the conduct of parliamentarians in relation to conflict of interest is an important public concern today. The Government has acted in this area following Chief Justice Parker's report and has introduced Bill C-l 14, the Senate and House of Commons Conflict of Interest Act as it is known.
Bill C-257 which we are debating this afternoon also relates to laws governing the conduct of Senators and Members of Parliament in relation to conflict of interest and to the Member for Moose Jaw's concern for that very important point when it comes to general subsidization to Members of Parliament, most specially with regard to the Special Grains Act.
Here we are dealing with existing provisions contained in the Senate and House of Commons Act which prohibit Senators and Members of Parliament from benefiting from any contract, agreement or commission of the Government of Canada which involves a payment of public money. Bill C-257
April 11, 1988

sponsored by the Member from Moose Jaw would change the prohibition against receiving public money contained in the Senate and House of Commons Act and make it apply only to contracts or agreements of sale or service. In my mind, such a change would immediately raise the issue of what the definition of a contract of sale or service would be. If the present exclusion of Senators and MPs is limited only to government contracts or sale or service, loopholes could possibly arise.
I understand the Member's objective that a parliamentarian should be able to receive government funding if he or she is a Member of a broad class of individuals, for example, farmers, eligible for financial assistance under a general government program. I think that this matter can be dealt with, however, without making the proposed changes to the Senate and House of Commons Act as proposed. Perhaps the most important point to make is that the present legislation does not disqualify Senators and Members of Parliament from receiving financial assistance from the Government for which a large number of Canadians can qualify. The key word in the Act is contract. Most general assistance programs sponsored by the Government of Canada do not, strictly speaking, involve a contract.
It is one thing for a Senator or a Member of Parliament to seek a contract with the Government in competition with other individuals or businesses which would lose out if the Senator or Member of Parliament were to get the contract. In this case, there could be a suspicion of conflict of interest. This is what the Senate and House of Commons Act is intended to prevent. If, however, a contract is not involved and the financial assistance, rather than being awarded on a competitive basis, is available to a class of individuals or businesses, there would be no possibility of conflict of interest.
I would submit that the Senate and House of Commons Act even now does not apply to such programs. Having said this, it is important to ensure that Section 20(1) of the present Act is properly administered so that the statutory clause prohibiting Members of Parliament from participating in or benefiting from any government contract, agreement or commission is not inserted in any general program of financial assistance.
I know that the Bill proposed by the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw is well intended that there is a clear understanding in connection with Members and with general assistance programs. I would also suggest, and I take heed of the suggestions made, that this motion go to a standing committee for study. Therefore, I move:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "that" and substituting the following therefor:

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to take a few moments to say a word on this Bill. Now that a motion has been moved, I think the Hon. Member
Senate and House of Commons Act
for Moose Jaw (Mr. Gottselig) would be able to speak again. I would be interested to know if he would be prepared to accept the motion put by his colleague. If he is satisfied with it, he will not get any argument from me or my colleagues. If he is not prepared to accept it, we are quite prepared to help him turn it down, although I think he is stuck. Even if he just gets the subject matter of his Bill before committee, then at least he has gotten that far.
I think that the Hon. Member is worrying too much. There are many others of his colleagues who should have been worried about conflict of interest. In this instance, I do not believe that the Hon. Member had a worry.
With government agricultural programs to which a farmer contributes, there is no problem, whether it is crop insurance, the Western Grain Stabilization Act or other programs. If a farmer contributes, he pays a premium to be covered.
In the case of the Special Grains Program, the Hon. Member as a farmer would of course have a direct interest in the matter, and, though I am no lawyer, I think that there is something in law about the rule of general application. If a program like the Special Grains Program is universal, then every farmer who holds a Wheat Board permit is eligible. It would not matter if the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw were a farmer, a Member of Parliament, an MLA, an alderman or a rural municipal councillor, or none of the above. He would be included under the umbrella of the general application of that particular law. That is why I think the Hon. Member was worrying too much.
If we were to follow the argument to its logical conclusion, then all of us would be in conflict of interest. For example, Members from all sides fight for improved old age pensions for which we are eligible. At the same time, MPs draw a pension as MPs if they have been here for six years or longer. One could conclude that there is a conflict there.
Corporate executives often come to this place. If a Member were to be on leave of absence from a corporation and his corporation, by taking advantage of a government program which meant millions and millions of dollars for the corporation, were to give him a better deal on his stock options, his dividends or his pension, he would be in a conflict of interest. That is why I think my hon. friend is worrying too much about this matter.
In any case, if this will make the Hon. Member or any other Hon. Members who come here from the farming or fishing communities feel more comfortable and more straightforward, that is fine. I have no problem with that. If that is all it will take to make them feel better, I am quite willing to help.
I wish to say something else as well. When I came here, I burned all my bridges behind me. I learned from other people who had been in this place years and years before me that if an MP is to do a full, good job representing his federal constituency, he does not have time for anything else. Some of my caucus

April 11, 1988
Senate and House of Commons Act
colleagues gave up their law practices, ministries or businesses completely to be Members of Parliament on a full-time basis.
A dear friend of mine served as a Member of Parliament for the old Kindersley constituency in the 1950s. After he had been here for about two or three years, he showed me the books for his farm. Ele was subsidizing the farm out of his MP's pay. That was in about 1955 when the pay was about $8,000 per year with about $1,500 per year expense allowance. Ele was subsidizing his farm out of MP's pay. I suspect, or at least I would not be surprised if the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw were doing the same damned thing right now. In the perception of the public, I believe that no one with a fair mind would think for one moment that the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw or anyone like him is in a conflict of interest.
I want to emphasize for all of us that if we decide to run for Parliament and if our constituents decide that we are the ones they want to be here on their behalf, we do not have time for anything else if we are to do a good job at it. I do not want to butt into the Hon. Member's private affairs, but I know that if I had a farm, I would sell it if I could find someone to buy it at a reasonable price, or I would have it incorporated. I would have no part whatsoever in it. The wife, the kids or a hired man would run it and I would have no part in it whatsoever. It would be at more than arm's length because the load is too heavy.
With the problems farmers are having nowadays along with the duties of a Member of Parliament who represents the thousands and thousands of square miles that the Hon. Member represents as well as 60,000 or 70,000 people, Members do not have time to worry about their farms. I just offer that as some free, unsolicited advice to my hon. friend from Moose Jaw, but I think it applies to all of us. We do not have time to run home for a couple or for three days a week to work on our real estate businesses, our insurance businesses or our law practices. If we are to do a half-decent job down here, we should not mix the two together. It does not work. I have seen too many who did not survive in this place for very long.
One of the reasons for the high turnaround here is that Members kept mixing one business with the other when the main reason they were here was to be Members of Parliament. If that is not their main business, they should quit. I know that that sounds harsh and hard, but I think that all of us here have a job, an honourable and worth-while profession. I think we all work very hard at governing ourselves accordingly.
Having given free advice to my hon. friend and having given my little lecture for the benefit of all of us, I want to say that I hope that the Government will at least agree to have this matter brought into committee. I hope it will also agree that any new conflict of interest guidelines will specifically include the rule of general application or universality for payments from the Government under any kind of program of this nature. If the Hon. Member's farm were eligible for $1,000 or $2,000 from the Special Grains Program and he had spent it
all on a wild time in Mexico, I would be a little leery. However, I know darn well that if he was eligible and did get any money, he sunk it all back into the farm and must put some more in. That is why he need not worry about conflict of interest in an instance such as this.
